$comment: Where 'true in general' and 'safe as done by a child in a kitchen' come apart. A caution is attached to a hazard, not restated per item, so the wording stays consistent across the whole chain. The game explains how these things work; it is not a method, and the wording must never imply otherwise.

botulism.label: Preserving is not a recipe you can eyeball
botulism.note: Fermenting and curing at home is real food science and it has a real failure mode. Clostridium botulinum grows in exactly the conditions these methods create — low oxygen, low acid, room temperature — and the toxin has no taste or smell. Salt concentration, acidity and temperature are not details; they are the whole safety margin. Follow a tested method from a food-safety authority, not a game.

caustic.label: Lye burns on contact
caustic.note: Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are strongly caustic. Both damage skin and eyes immediately and generate heat when they meet water. Historic soap-making is a good story and a bad first experiment.

peroxide_oxidizer.label: Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is a strong oxidiser
peroxide_oxidizer.note: Dilute solutions bleach hair and disinfect small cuts; concentrated ones react violently with organic material and burn skin on contact. It has to be kept in dark, vented containers, because light alone is enough to decompose it and build up pressure.

silver_nitrate_corrosive.label: Silver nitrate burns and stains on contact
silver_nitrate_corrosive.note: Concentrated solutions are corrosive enough that it is still used on purpose to cauterise tissue — the old name for it was 'lunar caustic'. Skin contact leaves a black stain as the silver reduces, and that stain does not wash off; it wears off only as the skin sheds.

fire.label: Fire and hot fat
fire.note: Cooking oil reaches temperatures that ignite, and water thrown into it will throw burning oil across a room. Never leave hot fat unattended, and never put water on an oil fire.

raw.label: Raw egg and unpasteurised milk
raw.note: Both can carry salmonella or listeria. The risk is small for most people and much larger if you are pregnant, very young, elderly, or immunocompromised.

alcohol.label: Alcohol
alcohol.note: Fermentation is how alcohol is made, and this part of the game explains that chemistry. It is not a brewing guide, and the drinking age where you live applies to you and not to the game.

cherry_kernel.label: The stone, not the fruit
cherry_kernel.note: Cherry flesh is entirely safe and this caution is not about eating cherries. The kernels inside the hard pits contain amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide when chewed or swallowed. Do not crack the stones open.

mercury_toxicity.label: Mercury is toxic, in the ore and in the metal
mercury_toxicity.note: Mercury and its compounds are toxic to the nervous system, immune system and kidneys, and both mining cinnabar and refining mercury from it are historic causes of mercury poisoning. Small-scale placer gold miners still use mercury to amalgamate gold from river sediment today, and it remains one of the largest ongoing sources of mercury pollution worldwide. This is chemistry to understand, not something to try at home.

mine_collapse.label: Pillars can fail without warning
mine_collapse.note: Room-and-pillar mines depend on the rock or coal pillars left standing to hold the roof up. When an array of pillars fails, it can happen with almost no warning and injure miners working well away from the collapse — a hazard mine-safety regulators still study and track.

mine_subsidence.label: Undermining a deposit can bring the surface down
mine_subsidence.note: Block caving lets a whole column of rock collapse under its own weight, and that collapse does not stop at the ore body — the ground above can sink into a crater-like depression, sometimes swallowing existing surface workings.

uranium_toxicity.label: Uranium is a heavy-metal poison first
uranium_toxicity.note: The main risk of exposure is chemical poisoning by uranium oxide rather than radioactivity — incorporated uranium accumulates in bone, liver, kidney and reproductive tissue. An excess risk of lung cancer has been documented among Navajo uranium miners specifically and linked to their occupation.

reactive_metal.label: These metals set fire to water
reactive_metal.note: Sodium forms flammable hydrogen and caustic sodium hydroxide on contact with water, and potassium reacts hard enough to ignite that hydrogen itself. Magnesium burns at around 3,100°C with a brilliant white light carrying strong ultraviolet. This is real chemistry, and none of it is a demonstration to improvise.

lead_toxicity.label: Lead is a neurotoxin
lead_toxicity.note: Lead is a neurotoxin that accumulates in soft tissue and bone. It damages the nervous system, interferes with biological enzymes, and can cause neurological problems ranging from behavioural issues to brain damage.

chlorine_gas.label: Chlorine gas is a poison, and was used as one
chlorine_gas.note: Elemental chlorine at high concentration is extremely dangerous and poisonous to most living organisms. It was the first gas deployed as a weapon, at the Second Battle of Ypres on 22 April 1915. This page is about where an industrial chemical comes from, and nothing on it is a method.

fluorine_hazard.label: Fluorine is why chemistry has martyrs
fluorine_hazard.note: Fluorine in its elemental form is highly toxic, and it reacts with almost every other element. Several nineteenth-century experimenters who tried to isolate it were injured or killed, and are remembered as the fluorine martyrs.

arsenic_toxicity.label: Arsenic is a poison, and a drinking-water problem
arsenic_toxicity.note: Arsenic compounds have been known since ancient times to be poisonous. The commonest cause of long-term exposure today is not deliberate — it is contaminated groundwater, and more than 200 million people worldwide are exposed to unsafe levels.

selenium_dose.label: Essential and toxic are the same element, at different doses
selenium_dose.note: Selenium is a required nutrient: the adult recommended intake is 55 micrograms a day and the tolerable upper limit is 400. Exceeding it causes selenosis. That is a narrow window compared with almost anything else on the shelf.

heavy_metal_dust.label: Some metals are only dangerous once they are dust
heavy_metal_dust.note: Cadmium is toxic and accumulates in the kidneys. Manganese overexposure causes manganism, a permanent movement disorder. Osmium tetroxide, which forms when osmium powder meets air, damages eyes and lungs at very low concentrations.

radioactivity.label: These are radioactive, and that is the point of some of them
radioactivity.note: Radium, thorium, plutonium and polonium are all radioactive. Radium was painted onto watch dials by women who wet the brushes with their lips, and many of them died of it — the Radium Girls case changed occupational-safety law. Polonium is acutely toxic in microgram amounts.

calcium_corrosive.label: Calcium metal burns skin on contact
calcium_corrosive.note: Calcium reacts with water faster than magnesium does, giving calcium hydroxide and hydrogen. Because that reaction is exothermic, calcium metal touching the moisture on skin causes severe corrosive irritation, and swallowing it does the same to the mouth, oesophagus and stomach.

lightning.label: Thunder is the sound of something already close
lightning.note: A lightning channel carries current through air heated to tens of thousands of degrees, and a strike does not have to hit a person to injure one — current spreads outward through the ground and through anything that conducts. Thunder is that channel being heard, so hearing it means the storm is already within range of it.

volcanic_activity.label: An erupting volcano kills at a distance
volcanic_activity.note: A pyroclastic flow can move at up to 700 km/h at around 1,000 °C, far too fast to outrun, and it is the most immediately lethal part of an eruption. Lava flows bury roads, farmland and buildings in their path; ash inhaled causes long-term respiratory harm, and heavy ashfall alone can collapse roofs. None of this is a hazard to work around up close.

earthquake_hazard.label: The shaking itself rarely kills — what falls on you does
earthquake_hazard.note: Most earthquake deaths come from collapsing buildings, falling debris and the fires and landslides a strong quake triggers, not from the ground motion itself. A major strike-slip rupture like the San Andreas Fault can move tens of feet in seconds, and aftershocks can bring down structures already weakened by the main shock for days afterward.

tsunami_hazard.label: A tsunami outruns a person on foot
tsunami_hazard.note: A tsunami crossing the open ocean travels as fast as a jet airliner and can arrive with almost no visible warning beyond the sea pulling back from the shore. The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake generated a tsunami that killed roughly 230,000 people across fourteen countries, most of whom had no warning system to tell them to move to higher ground.

severe_weather.label: Weather that kills people
severe_weather.note: Flood, storm surge, hurricane, blizzard, tornado and large hail are in this game because they are real physics, and they are the parts of that physics that kill. Moving floodwater carries and hides things and is far stronger than it looks; a blizzard removes visibility rather than merely reducing it; storm surge is the sea being pushed onto land; a tornado's winds can exceed 300 km/h in the strongest, rarest cases.

ozone.label: Ozone is not fresh air
ozone.note: The clean smell after a thunderstorm is a toxic gas. The same oxidising power that makes ozone useful for disinfecting is what damages mucous and respiratory tissue in animals, and plant tissue too, above about 0.1 ppm — around the level that already produces headaches and burning eyes.

methanol_toxicity.label: Methanol looks and smells like drinking alcohol
methanol_toxicity.note: It is difficult to tell methanol, ethanol and isopropyl alcohol apart by appearance or odour, and methanol is far more acutely toxic. The body turns it into formaldehyde and then formate, which shuts down the enzyme cells use to breathe. As little as 4 to 15 mL has reportedly caused irreversible optic nerve damage.

phenol_corrosive.label: Phenol degrades protein on contact
phenol_corrosive.note: Its corrosive effect on skin and mucous membrane comes from degenerating the protein itself, and prolonged contact can produce second and third-degree burns. It also passes into the blood through unbroken skin, and systemic poisoning can follow within minutes to hours.

formaldehyde_carcinogen.label: Formaldehyde is a carcinogen, not just a smell
formaldehyde_carcinogen.note: The International Agency for Research on Cancer reclassified formaldehyde as a known human carcinogen, associated with nasal sinus and nasopharyngeal cancer. Above about 0.1 ppm in air it irritates the eyes and mucous membranes. It is also what makes smoke-tanned hide keep, and what hardened the first casein plastics.

venomous_spur.label: The platypus is a venomous mammal
venomous_spur.note: The male carries a spur on each hind leg fed by a gland in the thigh, and the venom is powerful enough to inflict pain in humans — swelling, and a heightened sensitivity to pain that can last as long as months. It is largely defensin-like proteins, some of them unique to the species, and the spurs are weapons males use on each other.

lion_predation.label: Man-eating is a supplement, not a last resort
lion_predation.note: The Tsavo pair stopped the Uganda Railway in 1898; Patterson claimed 135 victims and a later review of his journal put it nearer 28–31. The modern figure is larger and less famous: more than 563 people killed in Tanzania since 1990 and at least 308 injured, with attacks peaking at harvest time. Studies of man-eating lions find that African lions eat people as a supplement to other food rather than because they are starving.

bear_defence.label: A defensive animal, not a predatory one
bear_defence.note: Brown bears seldom attack on sight and usually avoid people. What changes that is surprise or a threat to cubs: sows with cubs account for the majority of injuries and fatalities in North America. That is a different mechanism from a hunting animal, and it is why the danger is a function of distance and warning rather than of hunger.

rattlesnake_bite.label: A real venom, and a real treatment for it
rattlesnake_bite.note: About seven to eight thousand people are bitten by venomous snakes in the United States each year, and up to 95% of the snakebite deaths there are attributed to western and eastern diamondback rattlesnakes specifically. Antivenom, given intravenously, is effective at preventing death — but it works by binding and neutralising the venom enzymes already in the body, and it carries its own side effects. It is a hospital treatment, not a home one.

elephant_musth.label: A herbivore, dangerous for a reason that has nothing to do with diet
elephant_musth.note: Adult bulls enter a periodic state of raised testosterone called musth, marked by a fluid running from the temporal gland down the side of the face. Males become extremely aggressive during it, and working elephants in musth are chained until it passes. Human–elephant conflict kills as many as 80 people a year in Sri Lanka, where farmers kill more than 230 elephants in return.

road_animal.label: The dangerous ones are the ones you meet at speed
road_animal.note: Deer-vehicle collisions run to 500,000 a year in Europe and 1–1.5 million in North America, and together account for some 30,000 injuries and 200 deaths. Nine out of ten animal collisions in Australia involve kangaroos, which cross at around 50 km/h and are heavy enough to come through a windscreen. By comparison only two fatal kangaroo attacks have ever been reliably documented in Australia.

sting_anaphylaxis.label: The sting is a protein, and the reaction is an allergy
sting_anaphylaxis.note: Most stings produce a local reaction. An estimated 5–10% of people have a generalised systemic response instead, and in the United States about 40 people a year die of anaphylaxis from stinging-insect allergy. The mechanism is the same IgE pathway as a food allergy — a venom protein where a seed protein would be — which is why an insect sting and a peanut appear in the same part of a medical textbook.

thujone_toxicity.label: Thujone in concentrated sage oil
thujone_toxicity.note: Ordinary cooking with sage leaves is not the concern here. Sage essential oil contains α- and β-thujone, a neurotoxin that can cause convulsions in animals and severe intoxication in humans, which is why European regulators cap supplemental use at 6 mg a day. The leaf on a plate and the oil in a bottle are not the same dose.

bay_leaf_hazard.label: Bay leaves are for flavour, not for eating
bay_leaf_hazard.note: Bay leaves stay stiff even after long cooking and can pose a choking hazard or abrade the digestive tract if swallowed whole. They are meant to flavour a dish and be lifted back out before serving, never eaten.

niacin_flush.label: Niacin flush is a real, dose-triggered reaction
niacin_flush.note: Ordinary dietary niacin is not the concern here. More than 30 mg taken as a supplement can flush the face, arms and chest — vasodilation from a spike in prostaglandin and serotonin, usually gone in 15 to 30 minutes. Sustained-release niacin at medicinal doses (500 to 3,000 mg a day) carries a real risk of liver damage.

b6_neuropathy.label: Vitamin B6 neuropathy is a supplement-dose problem
b6_neuropathy.note: Ordinary dietary B6 is not the concern. Above roughly 1,000 mg a day, taken as a supplement over a long period, pyridoxine causes a painful, sometimes irreversible nerve damage — pain and numbness in the hands and feet, and in severe cases trouble walking. Regulators disagree sharply on where the safe ceiling is: the EU sets 12 mg a day, the US 100.

vitamin_e_bleeding.label: Vitamin E can potentiate blood thinners
vitamin_e_bleeding.note: Vitamin E from food is not the concern. Supplemental doses above roughly 300 mg a day can increase the anti-clotting action of aspirin, warfarin and other blood thinners, and the US upper intake limit of 1,000 mg a day was set from bleeding risk observed in animal studies.

eu_dye_hyperactivity_warning.label: The EU requires a warning label on this dye
eu_dye_hyperactivity_warning.note: Red 40, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6 are three of the 'Southampton Six' synthetic dyes an EU regulation, effective 2010, requires be labelled 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.' The underlying science is genuinely disputed: some studies link the dyes to hyperactivity in children, others do not, and the EU and US regulators have reached different conclusions from the same evidence.

yellow_5_allergy_warning.label: Yellow 5 carries its own FDA-mandated allergy warning
yellow_5_allergy_warning.note: The US FDA requires products containing tartrazine to state that it may cause allergic-type reactions, including bronchial asthma, in certain susceptible people — a separate concern from the EU attention warning above, and specific to Yellow 5 among the four dyes in this batch.

blue_1_enteral_advisory.label: A 2003 FDA advisory, and it is not about candy
blue_1_enteral_advisory.note: Ordinary food and drink use is not what this is about. In 2003 the FDA warned health care providers specifically about this dye's potential toxicity when used to tint enteral (feeding-tube) nutrition solutions, after reports of patient harm in that clinical context.

shiitake_dermatitis.label: Raw shiitake can cause a rash
shiitake_dermatitis.note: Rarely, eating shiitake raw or only lightly cooked triggers 'shiitake dermatitis' — a streaky, itchy rash that appears about 24 hours later, covering much of the body including the face and scalp. Cooking it through is the difference.

spirulina_contamination.label: Spirulina supplements and contamination
spirulina_contamination.note: Spirulina itself doesn't make toxins. But some supplements have tested positive for microcystins from co-occurring toxic blue-green algae, and China's food safety regulator found lead, mercury and arsenic widespread in spirulina supplements sold there. The organism is not the hazard; unregulated sourcing is.

synephrine_cardio.label: Synephrine carries ephedra's risk profile, not a safer one
synephrine_cardio.note: Marketed as the ephedra-free stimulant after ephedra was banned, bitter orange is believed to cause the same spectrum of adverse events. Case reports link it to stroke, myocardial infarction and angina; the NCCIH found little evidence it is actually safer.

caffeine_powder.label: Caffeine from coffee or tea is not the same risk as the pure powder
caffeine_powder.note: Caffeine from coffee or tea is not the concern here — the FDA still calls it generally recognized as safe, and a lethal dose that way is something like 75 to 100 cups. Pure powdered caffeine sold as a supplement is different: a level tablespoon can be a lethal dose, and it has killed people who measured by volume instead of a scale.

horsetail_thiaminase.label: Horsetail's thiaminase, over time
horsetail_thiaminase.note: Field horsetail contains thiaminase, an enzyme that breaks down vitamin B1. It is documented as toxic to livestock, particularly horses, when eaten over a long enough period — a dose-over-time problem, not an instant one.

aloin_laxative.label: Aloe's outer leaf layer is not the gel
aloin_laxative.note: Aloe vera's gel core is one thing; the outer leaf layer holds aloin, a bitter latex compound the FDA banned from over-the-counter laxatives in 2002. Oral ingestion of aloe extracts can cause abdominal pain, cramps, and hepatitis if taken chronically.

psyllium_choking.label: Psyllium needs water to go with it
psyllium_choking.note: Psyllium husk swells into mucilage on contact with liquid. Taken without enough water it can thicken in the throat and become a choking hazard, or form a bowel obstruction or bezoar further down.

fos_fodmap.label: FOS is a FODMAP
fos_fodmap.note: Fructooligosaccharides resist human digestive enzymes and are fermented by bacteria in the colon instead, producing gas. That fermentation is well tolerated by most people at ordinary doses, but not by people with Irritable Bowel Syndrome or FODMAP sensitivity.

ginseng_interactions.label: Ginseng interacts with medication
ginseng_interactions.note: Panax ginseng is generally considered safe for adults used under six months, but it can interact with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and its use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is considered potentially unsafe.

salmonella_illness.label: Salmonella causes real food poisoning
salmonella_illness.note: Nontyphoidal Salmonella infection generally causes gastroenteritis — food poisoning, in plain terms — and the US alone counts about 1,200,000 cases a year. Most healthy adults recover without incident; infants, the elderly, organ-transplant recipients and anyone immunocompromised are the ones genuinely at risk of it turning severe.

aspirin_reye.label: Reye syndrome links aspirin to a rare, severe childhood illness
aspirin_reye.note: About 90% of Reye syndrome cases in children are associated with aspirin (salicylate) use during a viral illness, which is why health guidance in the United States says aspirin should not be given to anyone under 19 during a fever-causing illness. The syndrome itself is rare — under one in a million children a year — but death occurs in 20 to 40% of those affected, and about a third of survivors are left with lasting brain damage.

streptomycin_ototoxicity.label: Streptomycin can cause permanent hearing and balance damage
streptomycin_ototoxicity.note: Like other aminoglycoside antibiotics, streptomycin's most concerning side effects are kidney and ear toxicity. Damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve can be transient or permanent, causing tinnitus, vertigo, loss of balance, or deafness — and use during pregnancy has been linked to permanent congenital deafness in the child.

insulin_hypoglycemia.label: Too much insulin is a medical emergency, not a dosing error to shrug off
insulin_hypoglycemia.note: Insulin in excess of what the body needs to handle the carbohydrate it has eaten causes hypoglycemic coma and can kill. Symptoms include dizziness, weakness, trembling, seizures, confusion and drowsiness, escalating to coma.

penicillin_allergy.label: Penicillin allergy is common to claim, rare to confirm
penicillin_allergy.note: About 10% of people in the United States report a penicillin allergy, but the great majority were never truly allergic or have outgrown it — skin-test positivity drops by about 10% with every year of avoidance, and roughly 90% of self-reported cases can eventually tolerate penicillin again. A true IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction is rare, occurring in roughly 0.01% of patients, though a milder rash affects 1 to 10%.

apricot_kernel.label: The kernel, not the flesh
apricot_kernel.note: Apricot flesh is entirely safe and this caution is not about eating apricots. The kernel inside the pit contains amygdalin — bitter kernels run about 5% amygdalin, sweet ones about 0.9% — which breaks down into cyanide. Do not eat the kernel.

rhubarb_leaf.label: The stalk, not the leaf
rhubarb_leaf.note: Rhubarb's stalk is what's eaten. The leaf blade contains oxalic acid, a nephrotoxin, and real poisonings have followed eating the leaves — including a wartime shortage-era recommendation in Britain that was later withdrawn.

bean_lectin.label: Raw beans are not a recipe you can eyeball
bean_lectin.note: Raw or undercooked common beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a toxic lectin — most concentrated in red kidney beans, but present across the species. A full rolling boil for at least 30 minutes destroys it; a slow cooker's lower heat does not.

cashew_shell.label: The shell is a poison-ivy relative
cashew_shell.note: Raw cashew shells and unroasted seeds carry anacardic acid, a potent skin-irritant resin chemically related to the toxin in poison ivy. Commercial cashews are always shelled and roasted or steamed before sale for exactly this reason.

cassava_cyanogenic_toxicity.label: Raw cassava is toxic — bitter varieties badly so
cassava_cyanogenic_toxicity.note: Cassava's roots, peel and leaves carry cyanogenic glycosides — mainly linamarin — that release hydrogen cyanide once the plant's own enzyme breaks them down, which is exactly what happens when it's chewed raw. Sweet varieties carry only a little; bitter varieties can carry fifty times as much, and need soaking, grating and fermenting for days before the toxin drops to a safe level, not just cooking. Long-term exposure to poorly processed cassava causes konzo, a real, irreversible paralytic disease still seen where processing is rushed.

cassia_coumarin.label: Cassia cinnamon carries far more coumarin than Ceylon
cassia_coumarin.note: Cassia cinnamon — the common supermarket kind — runs well over 1mg of coumarin per gram, sometimes far more; true Ceylon cinnamon carries only trace amounts. High coumarin intake over time risks liver and kidney harm.

nutmeg_myristicin.label: Nutmeg's own toxin, in excess
nutmeg_myristicin.note: Myristicin, nutmeg's own compound, is a toxin in pure form — consuming excessive amounts of nutmeg can cause real myristicin poisoning, not just an upset stomach.

ecoli_illness.label: E. coli is usually harmless, and sometimes isn't
ecoli_illness.note: Most E. coli strains are part of the normal gut microbiota and are harmless or even beneficial. Pathogenic strains are a different matter: some cause serious food poisoning, and virulent strains can cause gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, neonatal meningitis, and hemorrhagic colitis.

paracetamol_overdose.label: Paracetamol overdose is a leading cause of acute liver failure
paracetamol_overdose.note: Paracetamol is safe at the recommended dose and dangerous well before it tastes dangerous. Taking more than the maximum adult daily dose — three to four grams — can cause potentially fatal liver damage. Paracetamol toxicity is one of the leading causes of poisoning in high-income countries, and the single most common cause of acute liver failure in many of them.

cowpox_zoonosis.label: Cowpox still circulates — now mostly by way of cats
cowpox_zoonosis.note: Despite the name, cowpox's usual wild hosts are woodland rodents, particularly voles, not cattle. Domestic cats catch it from those rodents and can pass it on to their owners, which is how most human cowpox cases happen today.

histamine_scombroid.label: Histamine is also a real fish-poisoning toxin
histamine_scombroid.note: Above about 16°C, bacteria on improperly stored fish convert the histidine already in the flesh into histamine, and enough of it causes scombroid food poisoning: flushed skin, headache, itching and cramps, usually from tuna, mackerel or other dark-fleshed fish left too warm for too long.

shark_bite.label: Rare, but the numbers are real
shark_bite.note: Unprovoked bites are uncommon set against how many people swim in shark habitat, but they are documented: 351 unprovoked great white bites since 1580, 59 of them fatal, and the tiger shark ranks second worldwide for fatal attacks. Bull sharks are one of the three species most often implicated in bites on people, and oceanic whitetips were blamed for attacks on shipwreck survivors as recently as the 1945 sinking of the USS Indianapolis.

blue_ringed_octopus_bite.label: No antivenom exists for this bite
blue_ringed_octopus_bite.note: The bite itself is often painless, and the octopus is docile — there are no reported cases of it attacking a person unprovoked. But the tetrodotoxin it carries blocks nerve signal at the source, and without artificial respiration started fast enough a serious bite can be fatal within hours. There is no antivenom; the only treatment is life support until the toxin clears the body on its own.

box_jellyfish_sting.label: The most venomous animal most people never see
box_jellyfish_sting.note: Chironex fleckeri, the largest box jellyfish species, has caused at least 79 recorded deaths since 1883, and a severe sting can bring on cardiac arrest within two minutes. Most encounters with box jellyfish are far milder than that worst case, but the ones that are not do not leave time to look up a treatment.

venomous_fish_sting.label: A real venom, and a real treatment for it
venomous_fish_sting.note: Stonefish carry the most potent venom of any fish known — stings have caused documented deaths in Australia and Japan, and stonefish antivenom is the second most-administered antivenom in Australia. Lionfish deliver a milder but genuine venom through long dorsal spines; it rarely kills a healthy adult but has killed young children, the elderly, and people allergic to it. For both, hot water above 45°C denatures the venom and is the standard field first aid, alongside proper medical care.

piranha_bite.label: Rare, and rarely serious — but real
piranha_bite.note: The pack-hunter reputation is mostly myth, and unprovoked attacks on people are uncommon. But piranhas do bite: incidents at crowded swimming spots in Brazil and Argentina have sent dozens of people to hospital with foot and heel wounds in a single day, mostly minor, occasionally needing stitches. Fatal attacks are exceptionally rare.

scorpion_sting.label: Real venom, and it varies a lot by species
scorpion_sting.note: Most scorpion stings cause pain and swelling and nothing worse. A handful of genera in the family Buthidae are the exception — Androctonus and Leiurus in North Africa and the Middle East, Centruroides in Mexico, Tityus in South America — with venom that can be medically serious. Scorpion stings are estimated to cause around 3,000 deaths a year worldwide, concentrated in the regions those genera live.

tick_borne_disease.label: A real disease risk, tied to how long it feeds
tick_borne_disease.note: Ixodes ticks are the main carrier of Lyme disease, and transmission risk rises sharply the longer a tick stays attached to its host, with most studies putting the threshold around 24 hours. Even so, only an estimated 1.2 to 1.4% of recognised tick bites result in Lyme disease, and people treated with antibiotics within days of the first symptoms have the best outcomes.

mistletoe_toxicity.label: Mistletoe berries and leaves are toxic if eaten
mistletoe_toxicity.note: American mistletoe contains phoratoxins that can cause blurred vision, nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, though the US National Capital Poison Center notes severe reactions are rare and usually limited to minor stomach upset. European mistletoe contains viscumin (a lectin) which at high doses can disrupt protein synthesis in cells. Both berries and leaves carry the risk, across species.

bracken_ptaquiloside.label: Bracken fern carries a documented carcinogen
bracken_ptaquiloside.note: Pteridium aquilinum contains ptaquiloside, linked to haemorrhagic disease and tumours in grazing livestock, and to elevated stomach and oesophageal cancer risk in human populations where the young fronds are traditionally eaten. The compound is water-soluble and breaks down with soaking, boiling, or age.

amatoxin_poisoning.label: The deadliest mushroom, and a real cause of death every year
amatoxin_poisoning.note: Amanita phalloides causes roughly 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Its amatoxins are thermostable — cooking or freezing does nothing to them — and as little as half a cap can be a lethal dose. Symptoms are deceptively delayed: gastrointestinal illness appears 6 to 12 hours in and eases for a few days before liver and kidney failure follow.

muscimol_toxicity.label: Psychoactive, and a real poisoning risk
muscimol_toxicity.note: Amanita muscaria's muscimol and ibotenic acid bring on vomiting, delirium and altered consciousness at roughly the dose in one cap. The North American Mycological Association has found no reliably documented death from it in the past century, but that is not the same as safe to eat — this game explains the chemistry, it is not a foraging guide.

morel_raw_toxicity.label: Morels are toxic raw
morel_raw_toxicity.note: True morels contain thermolabile toxins and must always be cooked before eating — consuming them raw is specifically discouraged. Even properly cooked morels can reportedly upset the stomach when eaten alongside alcohol.

puffball_amanita_confusion.label: A deadly Amanita's 'egg' stage can look like a young puffball
puffball_amanita_confusion.note: Puffballs are eaten only while young and solid white all the way through. That same immature stage is exactly how a death cap or other deadly Amanita first looks, sliced open from its 'egg' — foraging guides insist on checking the inside of every puffball before eating it, precisely because of that resemblance.

beryllium_disease.label: Beryllium dust causes a chronic lung disease
beryllium_disease.note: Inhaled beryllium-containing dust is toxic and can cause berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease), a life-threatening allergic lung condition that can progress to pulmonary fibrosis and heart failure. This applies to the ore as much as the refined metal — commercial beryllium handling requires dedicated dust control.

chrysotile_asbestos.label: Some serpentine is asbestos
chrysotile_asbestos.note: Chrysotile, a fibrous form of serpentine, is one of the most important asbestos minerals. Breaking or excavating serpentine rock that contains it can release asbestos fibres into the air, a long-term lung health hazard from inhalation.

malaria_burden.label: Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands a year
malaria_burden.note: In 2024 an estimated 282 million malaria cases caused around 610,000 deaths, about 95% of them in sub-Saharan Africa. The fever itself comes from red blood cells bursting in near-synchrony as the parasite completes each replication cycle.

toxoplasmosis_risk.label: Usually silent, but not always harmless
toxoplasmosis_risk.note: Toxoplasma gondii infection is generally asymptomatic in healthy adults, and up to half the world's population may carry it without ever knowing. Infants infected before birth and anyone immunocompromised face real risk of serious illness.

giardiasis_illness.label: A few swallowed cysts are enough
giardiasis_illness.note: Ingesting only a handful of Giardia cysts can start an infection, and in some developing countries as much as 30% of the population carries it. Illness is usually gastrointestinal and self-limiting, not life-threatening.

amoebiasis_illness.label: A real, sometimes fatal dysentery
amoebiasis_illness.note: Entamoeba histolytica infects an estimated 35 to 50 million people worldwide and is thought to kill more than 55,000 of them a year, mostly through amoebic dysentery or a liver abscess.

trichomoniasis_sti.label: A common sexually transmitted infection
trichomoniasis_sti.note: Trichomonas vaginalis causes an estimated 160 million infections a year worldwide. Most people who carry it, roughly 85% of women and 77% of men, have no symptoms at all, but it still spreads person to person through sexual contact.

cryptosporidiosis_illness.label: Resists the chlorine that stops most water contaminants
cryptosporidiosis_illness.note: Cryptosporidium's oocysts are highly resistant to ordinary chlorine disinfection, which has made it a real cause of large waterborne outbreaks. Illness is usually watery diarrhea, worse and longer-lasting in anyone immunocompromised.

soil_transmitted_helminths.label: The leading cause of anemia in developing countries
soil_transmitted_helminths.note: Ascaris, hookworm, and pinworm are among the most common human parasitic infections worldwide — hookworm alone is closely associated with poverty and is the leading cause of anemia and undernutrition where it's endemic.

trichinosis_illness.label: From undercooked meat, sometimes seriously
trichinosis_illness.note: Trichinosis symptoms can start within twelve hours of eating meat carrying Trichinella's encysted larvae. Most cases are mild, but heavy larval loads can cause serious muscle and cardiac complications.

lymphatic_filariasis_burden.label: Chronic swelling that builds over repeated exposure
lymphatic_filariasis_burden.note: Around 40 million people live with lymphatic filariasis, the disfiguring swelling of elephantiasis among its most severe forms. The damage comes from adult worms physically obstructing the lymphatic system, and it accumulates with repeated infection rather than appearing all at once.

tapeworm_infection.label: Large, long-lived, and usually mild
tapeworm_infection.note: Taenia solium and Taenia saginata are among the largest parasites that infect humans — the beef tapeworm can exceed 22 metres and live in a person for 25 years. Most infections cause mild or no symptoms, detected only when a segment passes.

schistosomiasis_burden.label: The second-most devastating parasitic disease, after malaria
schistosomiasis_burden.note: The World Health Organization considers schistosomiasis the second-most socioeconomically devastating parasitic disease after malaria. An estimated 600 to 700 million people live at risk of it, and eggs trapped in tissue are what cause most of the lasting damage.

liver_fluke_infection.label: A parasite that can live in one host for decades
liver_fluke_infection.note: Clonorchis sinensis, the Chinese liver fluke, can survive around 30 years in a single human host after being eaten in raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Long-term infection is linked to chronic liver and bile-duct disease.

body_louse_disease_vector.label: A real historical epidemic-disease carrier
body_louse_disease_vector.note: Body lice can transmit epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, and trench fever between people — diseases that caused massive historical outbreaks in crowded, unsanitary conditions such as wartime trenches and refugee camps.

scabies_infestation.label: Intensely itchy, and it spreads easily
scabies_infestation.note: Scabies mites spread readily through skin contact and are common in crowded settings such as care homes, schools, refugee camps, prisons, and hospitals. The infestation itself is rarely dangerous, but it is intensely itchy and highly contagious.

head_lice_infestation.label: Extremely common, not a sign of poor hygiene
head_lice_infestation.note: Head lice spread through direct head-to-head contact and cause millions of treated cases every year in the US alone. They're a nuisance, not a health danger — lice do not spread disease the way body lice can.

crocodilian_bite.label: Real predators, and real numbers
crocodilian_bite.note: The Nile crocodile is estimated to cause 275 to 745 attacks a year, about 63% of them fatal — more human deaths than every other crocodilian species combined. The American alligator bites far less often and far less often fatally, but its measured bite force is among the strongest of any living animal. Both are ambush predators, not something to test at the water's edge.

king_cobra_venom.label: The longest venomous snake alive
king_cobra_venom.note: A single bite can deliver several hundred milligrams of venom, and an untreated bite can kill in as little as 30 minutes. Confirmed human bites are rare — only a handful of clinical cases appear in the medical literature — but a polyvalent antivenom exists in India for when one occurs.

komodo_dragon_bite.label: A genuinely venomous bite, not just a dirty mouth
komodo_dragon_bite.note: For decades the danger of a Komodo dragon bite was blamed on bacteria in its mouth; 2009 research instead found dedicated venom glands secreting toxic proteins. Komodo National Park recorded 24 attacks on people between 1974 and 2012, 5 of them fatal — rare, but the largest living lizard is a genuine apex predator on its home islands.

gila_monster_venom.label: Real venom, very rarely dangerous
gila_monster_venom.note: The only lizard native to the United States that is venomous, delivering it by chewing rather than injecting. It is not generally dangerous to a healthy adult — only one confirmed fatality has been recorded since 1930. A compound unique to its saliva, exendin-4, became the basis of a real class of diabetes medication.

poison_dart_frog_toxin.label: The most toxic vertebrate known by weight
poison_dart_frog_toxin.note: A single wild golden poison frog carries an estimated one milligram of batrachotoxin on its skin — enough, by weight, to kill 10 to 20 adult humans. The toxin is diet-derived: frogs raised away from their natural wild diet lose it entirely. The Emberá people of Colombia have used it to tip blowdarts for generations.

cane_toad_toxin.label: Poison in the skin, real risk to pets
cane_toad_toxin.note: When threatened, a cane toad's shoulder glands secrete a milky bufotoxin. Dogs that bite or mouth one are especially at risk — drooling, red gums and seizures call for a vet immediately — and human deaths from consuming the toad have been recorded, though they are rare.

salamander_toxin.label: A real neurotoxin, right on the skin
salamander_toxin.note: The fire salamander's black-and-yellow pattern warns of samandarin, a neurotoxin secreted from glands on its skin that is toxic to the mammals, birds and fish that try to eat it. No antidote exists, though ordinary handling with unbroken skin poses little risk to a person.

polar_bear_attack.label: A predator, not a defensive animal
polar_bear_attack.note: A peer-reviewed survey found 73 confirmed polar bear attacks across all five range countries from 1870 to 2014, killing 20 people and injuring 63. Nutritionally stressed adult males were the most common attackers, and in most cases the bear was acting as a predator rather than defending itself or cubs — a different mechanism from a brown bear's usual defensive attack.

big_cat_attack.label: Rare, but the history is real
big_cat_attack.note: Unprovoked attacks on people are uncommon for either species, but both have documented cases: the 'Leopard of Rudraprayag' killed more than 125 people in India before being shot in 1926, and confirmed cougar attacks in North America rose from 53 between 1890 and 1990 to 88 by 2004, with about 20 deaths recorded over that span.

coyote_attack.label: Rare, and rarely serious — but real
coyote_attack.note: Coyotes are shy around people, and confirmed attacks are uncommon: 367 documented in the US and Canada between 1977 and 2015, most of them minor. Two are confirmed fatal — a 3-year-old in 1981 and an adult in 2009 — the only known deaths from an unprovoked coyote attack on record.

chimpanzee_attack.label: Strength enough to cause severe injury
chimpanzee_attack.note: A chimpanzee's strength and sharp teeth mean an attack, even on an adult human, can cause severe and disfiguring injury — one well-documented case cost the victim her hands, eyes, nose and part of her jaw. Wild chimps rarely target people; nearly every serious case on record involves a captive or formerly captive animal.

tailings_dam_failure.label: A tailings dam can fail catastrophically
tailings_dam_failure.note: Tailings dams hold back millions of tonnes of waste slurry, often built up in stages from the tailings themselves. When one fails, the release can travel for kilometres in minutes — the Brumadinho dam collapse in Brazil in January 2019 killed 272 people.

cyanide_poisoning.label: Cyanide is lethal in small doses
cyanide_poisoning.note: Sodium cyanide dissolved in water is what leaches gold out of ore, and it is genuinely lethal — plants have to keep the solution alkaline, above pH 10.5, specifically to stop toxic hydrogen cyanide gas from forming. The 2000 Baia Mare spill in Romania, when a tailings dam holding cyanide solution failed and released it into the Tisza river, killed enormous numbers of fish across three countries. This is industrial chemistry, not something to handle casually.

blasting_hazard.label: Blasting is a controlled explosion, not a safe one
blasting_hazard.note: ANFO and other blasting agents are designed to fragment solid rock, and the same holes and timing that make a blast predictable can misfire, throw flyrock well beyond the blast area, or detonate early if handled wrong. Mine blasting crews follow strict exclusion zones and licensing for exactly this reason.

hotbox.label: Overheated bearings start real fires
hotbox.note: The term comes from journal-bearing axleboxes packed with oil-soaked waste to cut friction. When the oil ran dry the bearing overheated and could set the whole car alight before anyone noticed — trackside hot-box detectors, and later roller bearings, were built specifically to catch and prevent it.

airship_hydrogen.label: Hydrogen lift is real, and it really burns
airship_hydrogen.note: Hydrogen is flammable across a huge range of concentrations in air, and needs very little energy to ignite. The Hindenburg's hydrogen-filled envelope caught fire on landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey on 6 May 1937, killing 36 people — the reason every airship built since switched to inert helium instead.

mri_magnetic_field.label: A magnetic field strong enough to make metal fly
mri_magnetic_field.note: An MRI magnet's field is always on, tens of thousands of times Earth's, and it does not turn off between patients. A loose ferromagnetic object — an oxygen tank, a chair, a tool left in a pocket — can be pulled across the room and become a lethal projectile, which is why screening happens before anyone enters.

pet_radiotracer.label: A radioactive tracer, injected on purpose
pet_radiotracer.note: FDG carries fluorine-18, a real radioisotope, directly into the bloodstream. A clinical PET scan uses a dose weighed and justified by a physician against the diagnostic benefit — not a quantity to approximate outside medical supervision.

nitroglycerin_instability.label: Unstabilised nitroglycerin can detonate on its own
nitroglycerin_instability.note: Nitroglycerin can detonate from shock, friction or heat with almost no warning, which is exactly why its own discoverer, Ascanio Sobrero, was horrified at the idea of weaponising it after he first made it in 1846. It killed and maimed people in transport and storage for twenty years before Alfred Nobel found a way to stabilise it into dynamite. This is industrial chemistry, not something to make or handle.

high_explosive_hazard.label: TNT and dynamite are designed to detonate
high_explosive_hazard.note: TNT and dynamite are real high explosives, engineered to detonate reliably on command with a blasting cap. Both were part of the cargo when a munitions ship collided in Halifax harbour in 1917 and detonated, killing at least 1,782 people in the largest human-made explosion before the nuclear age. Making, storing or handling either is licensed, regulated work.

gunpowder_hazard.label: Black powder ignites easily and burns explosively fast
gunpowder_hazard.note: Gunpowder ignites from a spark, flame or even friction, and once confined it burns fast enough to act as an explosive rather than a controlled fire. A gunpowder store igniting in Delft in 1654 — the 'Delft Thunderclap' — killed at least 100 people and levelled a large part of the city, which is why powder magazines have been built isolated and underground ever since. It is real energetic chemistry, not a firework to make at home.

blasting_cap_hazard.label: A detonator's whole job is to go off from a small shock
blasting_cap_hazard.note: Mercury fulminate and other primary explosives used in blasting caps detonate from a shock or friction far too small to set off the explosive charge they trigger — that sensitivity is the point of a detonator, and it is also why they are made and stored in tiny quantities, kept apart from the explosive itself until the moment of use. This is licensed industrial chemistry, not something to make or handle.

tropane_alkaloid_poisoning.label: Deadly nightshade, datura and angel's trumpet are true poisons
tropane_alkaloid_poisoning.note: Atropa belladonna, Datura stramonium and Brugmansia all carry tropane alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine) in every tissue, seeds and root most concentrated. Symptoms include dilated pupils, dry mouth, delirium, tachycardia and hallucinations; a fatal adult dose can be as few as 10-20 seeds' worth. Severe intoxication is a medical emergency treated with physostigmine.

coniine_poisoning.label: Poison hemlock killed Socrates
coniine_poisoning.note: Conium maculatum's coniine paralyses the respiratory muscles from the extremities inward, leaving the victim conscious to the end -- the death Plato describes in the Phaedo. It resembles several edible carrot-family plants closely enough that misidentification is the main real-world risk.

cicutoxin_poisoning.label: Water hemlock's root is North America's most violent plant poison
cicutoxin_poisoning.note: Cicutoxin attacks the central nervous system directly, causing seizures within 15-60 minutes of ingesting the root -- widely cited as the most acutely toxic native plant in North America. It has repeatedly been mistaken for edible wild parsnip.

ricin_toxicity.label: Ricin is one of the most toxic substances known
ricin_toxicity.note: Ricinus communis's seed contains ricin, a ribosome-inactivating protein; the lethal dose in adults is considered to be four to eight seeds, though actual poisonings are relatively rare in practice since intact raw seeds are poorly absorbed unless chewed. Purified ricin has also been used as a poisoning weapon historically.

cardiac_glycoside_poisoning.label: Oleander and lily of the valley stop hearts, not just upset stomachs
cardiac_glycoside_poisoning.note: Both plants carry cardiac glycosides that slow the heart rate toward arrest by disrupting electrolyte balance; sinus bradycardia down to 50-60 beats per minute is the documented pattern in poisoning. The same chemistry, at controlled doses, treats congestive heart failure in conventional and traditional medicine alike.

aconitine_poisoning.label: Aconite is called the queen of poisons for a reason
aconitine_poisoning.note: Aconitum's aconitine acts on sodium channels in nerve and heart tissue; there is no antidote, and historic use on arrow tips and as wolf bait reflects its potency. Every part of the plant, including root and nectar, carries the toxin.

colchicine_toxicity.label: Colchicine's therapeutic and lethal doses sit close together
colchicine_toxicity.note: Colchicum autumnale is the original source of colchicine, still prescribed for gout, but the margin between an effective dose and a fatal one is narrow and there is no specific antidote. Its bitter bulb has been fatally mistaken for an onion.

podophyllotoxin_toxicity.label: Mayapple's rhizome is a powerful, unpredictable purgative
podophyllotoxin_toxicity.note: Podophyllum peltatum's podophyllotoxin is cytostatic -- it halts cell division, the same property later exploited in the chemotherapy drug etoposide -- and excessive ingestion of the rhizome or resin can cause severe catharsis, coma or death. The ripe fruit alone is considered edible.

taxine_poisoning.label: Yew is toxic in every part except the aril
taxine_poisoning.note: Taxus needles and seeds carry taxine alkaloids that can cause cardiac arrest; even chewing the leaves can trigger a severe reaction, and there is no antidote. Only the sweet, fleshy red aril around the seed is safe to eat -- the seed inside it is not.

phytolacca_toxicity.label: Pokeweed's root is far more toxic than its berry
phytolacca_toxicity.note: Phytolacca americana's phytolaccatoxin and related saponins are concentrated in the root; a mild dose is typically self-limiting nausea and vomiting, but heavier ingestion has caused low blood pressure and dangerous heart rhythm changes. Young leaves are eaten only after repeated boiling with water changes.

larkspur_toxicity.label: Larkspur is the leading cause of cattle poisoning on western rangeland
larkspur_toxicity.note: Delphinium's methyllycaconitine and related diterpenoid alkaloids cause convulsions and respiratory paralysis; there is no antidote, though most human exposures are minor because the plant tastes acrid and bitter.

furanocoumarin_phototoxicity.label: Giant hogweed's sap burns only where sunlight reaches it
furanocoumarin_phototoxicity.note: Heracleum mantegazzianum's furanocoumarins bind skin's DNA and only become damaging once activated by ultraviolet light -- phytophotodermatitis -- producing burns and blistering that can leave skin light-sensitive for months or years. Related, milder Apiaceae like cow parsnip and angelica share the same chemistry at lower concentration.

strychnine_poisoning.label: Strychnine causes death by asphyxiation through muscle convulsion
strychnine_poisoning.note: Strychnos nux-vomica's strychnine blocks an inhibitory spinal neurotransmitter, so every muscle in the body contracts at once; death, when it occurs, is from respiratory exhaustion. It remains sold commercially as a rodent poison.

grayanotoxin_honey.label: "Mad honey" from rhododendron nectar is a documented, ancient hazard
grayanotoxin_honey.note: Grayanotoxin from some rhododendron species' nectar passes into honey made from it; Xenophon's Anabasis records Greek soldiers disabled by eating it in Anatolia in 401 BC. Modern cases are usually self-limiting nausea and low blood pressure, rarely fatal.

nicotine_toxicity.label: Nicotine is acutely toxic in concentrated or pure form
nicotine_toxicity.note: A widely repeated 40-60 mg lethal-dose figure for nicotine was debunked in a 2014 reassessment; the real lower limit for a fatal outcome is estimated at 500-1000 mg. Nicotine is still absorbed readily through skin as well as the lungs -- a real hazard in tobacco harvesting known as green tobacco sickness, and in concentrated liquid form. Smoked tobacco's dominant long-term harm, however, is cumulative: addiction and the cancers linked to chronic use.

cocaine_dependency.label: Refined cocaine is addictive in a way chewed coca leaf is not
cocaine_dependency.note: Chewing raw coca leaf, buffered with lime, has no strong documented history of dependence; concentrating the leaf's alkaloid into cocaine hydrochloride or freebase produces a drug with high addiction potential and real cardiovascular, respiratory and stroke risk with chronic use.

opioid_overdose.label: Opium poppy alkaloids depress breathing at high doses
opioid_overdose.note: Morphine and the other opiates in opium poppy latex are central nervous system depressants; at doses above the therapeutic range they slow and eventually stop breathing, the mechanism behind opioid overdose deaths. The same chemistry, at controlled doses, remains medicine's benchmark pain reliever.

betel_nut_carcinogen.label: Habitual betel-nut chewing is linked to oral cancer
betel_nut_carcinogen.note: Areca catechu's arecoline is a mild stimulant on its own, but habitual chewers of betel quid are documented to be at substantially higher risk of oral cancer, and the practice can also cause tooth and gum disease. Effects are dose- and habit-dependent, not acute.

ayahuasca_mao_interaction.label: Ayahuasca's MAO inhibitors interact dangerously with some medicines
ayahuasca_mao_interaction.note: Banisteriopsis caapi's beta-carboline alkaloids inhibit monoamine oxidase; combined with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs this can trigger a hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome. The interaction, not the plant alone, is the acute risk.

sweet_flag_carcinogen.label: Sweet flag's beta-asarone is banned from US food products
sweet_flag_carcinogen.note: Acorus calamus rhizome contains cis-isoasarone and beta-asarone, shown to be carcinogenic to laboratory animals with long-term exposure; the FDA has banned its use as a food additive in the United States since 1968, though other countries still sell it.

mescal_bean_toxicity.label: Mescal bean seeds can cause convulsions and respiratory paralysis
mescal_bean_toxicity.note: Sophora secundiflora's bright red seeds concentrate cytisine, an alkaloid that in serious overdose can cause convulsions and paralysis of the respiratory muscles; fatalities are rare but the seed's toxicity is why it was historically replaced by peyote in vision-seeking ritual once peyote's milder profile became known.

morning_glory_seed_treatment.label: Commercial morning glory seeds are often chemically treated
morning_glory_seed_treatment.note: Garden-centre morning glory seeds are frequently coated with fungicides, pesticides, or historically methylmercury to prevent spoilage and pest damage -- a real, separate hazard from the seed's own LSA content, which alone has comparatively low toxicity.

methane_explosion.label: Methane is explosive in air
methane_explosion.note: Methane mixed with air ignites easily and burns explosively fast — "firedamp" was historically the leading cause of coal-mining disasters, and it is why modern gas appliances are built with strict safety standards.

hydrogen_flammability.label: Hydrogen has one of the widest explosive ranges of any gas
hydrogen_flammability.note: Hydrogen mixed with air is flammable across an unusually wide range, from about 4% to 75% hydrogen by volume, and detonable from about 18% to 59% — and it ignites with roughly a tenth of the energy needed to ignite a gasoline-air mixture. Its flame burns pale blue, close to invisible in daylight, which is part of why the 1937 Hindenburg disaster is still the substance's best-known incident.

hypoglycin_poisoning.label: Unripe akee is toxic — "Jamaican vomiting sickness"
hypoglycin_poisoning.note: Unripe akee arils and the fruit's inedible parts contain hypoglycin A and B, toxins that block the body's ability to make glucose and can cause severe, sometimes fatal vomiting sickness. The fruit is only safe once its own capsule has split open naturally on the tree; forcing it open early leaves the toxin concentration unsafe.

corrosive_acid.label: Strong acids burn on contact
corrosive_acid.note: Concentrated hydrochloric and sulfuric acid damage skin and eyes immediately on contact, and both can release dangerous fumes or heat if mishandled. This page is about where these acids come from and what industry uses them for, not a method for handling them.

carbon_tetrachloride_toxicity.label: Carbon tetrachloride damages the liver and kidneys
carbon_tetrachloride_toxicity.note: Carbon tetrachloride is toxic with repeated exposure, a suspected human carcinogen, and an ozone-depleting substance with an atmospheric lifetime of roughly 85 years. It was withdrawn from consumer products once these effects were understood — this page describes chemistry history, not a substance to keep around.

barium_toxicity.label: Soluble barium salts are toxic if swallowed
barium_toxicity.note: Barium nitrate and other soluble barium compounds block the potassium channels muscle and nerve cells depend on, driving potassium out of the blood and, in severe cases, causing paralysis or fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Insoluble barium sulfate is harmless by comparison — solubility is what makes a barium compound dangerous.

hexavalent_chromium.label: Hexavalent chromium is a recognised carcinogen
hexavalent_chromium.note: Sodium chromate and dichromate carry chromium in its +6 oxidation state, which the IARC classes as a Group 1 human carcinogen and which is regulated as a drinking-water contaminant — the compound at the centre of the Hinkley, California case made famous by Erin Brockovich. Chromium(III), the oxide this game reaches it from, is a different, far less hazardous oxidation state.

hydrofluoric_hazard.label: Hydrofluoric acid injures before it hurts
hydrofluoric_hazard.note: Unlike most acids, dilute hydrofluoric acid barely stings on contact, so a splash can go unnoticed while the fluoride ion penetrates skin and binds calcium in the blood and underlying bone. Burns are treated with calcium gluconate, not just rinsing, and a hand-sized splash of concentrated acid has been fatal. This is industrial chemistry to understand, not to handle casually.

strong_oxidizer_acid.label: Chlorine's stronger oxoacids are real oxidiser hazards
strong_oxidizer_acid.note: Chlorate, perchlorate and chlorine dioxide chemistry is genuinely dangerous in concentrated or dried form: these compounds are powerful oxidisers that can react explosively with organic material, metals or reducing agents. Perchloric acid work is done only in dedicated, water-washed fume hoods for exactly this reason, and sodium chlorate weedkiller has caused real poisonings and fires when stored carelessly.

oxalic_acid_toxicity.label: Oxalic acid is a real poison, not just a rhubarb-leaf curiosity
oxalic_acid_toxicity.note: Concentrated oxalic acid is corrosive and toxic if swallowed — it precipitates calcium out of the blood the same way it does in rhubarb-leaf poisoning, and industrial safety sheets treat it as a genuine hazard, not just a kitchen warning.

hexavalent_chromium_carcinogen.label: Hexavalent chromium is a confirmed carcinogen
hexavalent_chromium_carcinogen.note: Chromium(VI) compounds -- sodium chromate and dichromate among them -- are IARC Group 1 carcinogens, most dangerously when airborne and inhaled. Ingestion causes cancer of the mouth and small intestine and damages the liver. The same chemistry, leaked into groundwater from a cooling-tower additive, was the contamination behind the Hinkley, California case that made Erin Brockovich famous. It is also directly corrosive to eyes.

acetaldehyde_carcinogen.label: Acetaldehyde is what your body already makes from alcohol
acetaldehyde_carcinogen.note: The IARC classifies acetaldehyde associated with the consumption of alcoholic beverages as a Group 1 human carcinogen. It occurs naturally in ripe fruit, coffee and bread, and every drink of ethanol is turned into it by the liver before being broken down further -- concentrated acetaldehyde itself is simply more of the same acutely irritant, carcinogenic substance.

perc_solvent_toxicity.label: Perc is a probable carcinogen, not just a dry-cleaning smell
perc_solvent_toxicity.note: The EPA and IARC classify tetrachloroethylene as a probable human carcinogen. Exposure harms the nervous system, liver, kidneys and reproductive system, and decades of research have pushed the dry-cleaning industry to look for replacements.

oxidizer_hazard.label: Strong oxidisers burn on contact and burn what they touch
oxidizer_hazard.note: Concentrated hydrogen peroxide and sodium chlorate are both powerful oxidisers -- a world apart from the dilute 3% antiseptic or the trace exposure most people ever see. A dose of only a few grams of chlorate is lethal, destroying red blood cells' ability to carry oxygen; concentrated peroxide is corrosive enough to burn skin on contact and was once flown as rocket propellant for exactly that reactivity.

nickel_dermatitis.label: Nickel is the most common metal allergy there is
nickel_dermatitis.note: Soluble nickel salts like nickel nitrate and nickel acetate are more readily absorbed through skin than the metal itself, and nickel contact allergy is the single most common metal sensitisation in humans -- a rash from a cheap watch strap and an industrial soluble-nickel exposure are the same underlying immune reaction, just different doses.

phosgene_toxicity.label: Phosgene killed more people than any other WWI gas
phosgene_toxicity.note: Phosgene is colourless and, at first, faintly grass-smelling — deceptive, because its worst damage to the lungs is delayed for hours after exposure. It caused roughly 85,000 of the deaths from gas warfare in the First World War, more than any other agent used, and it remains an important industrial chemical today, made and consumed immediately on-site rather than stored or shipped.

bleach_fumes.label: Bleach mixed with acid or ammonia makes toxic gas
bleach_fumes.note: Sodium hypochlorite solutions, such as liquid bleach, release toxic chlorine gas when mixed with an acid such as vinegar. Mixed instead with ammonia, ammonium salts, urea or other amines, it produces chloramines — both classes of gaseous product can cause acute lung injury. This is why cleaning products are never mixed.

ammonium_nitrite_instability.label: Ammonium nitrite can explode when heated
ammonium_nitrite_instability.note: Ammonium nitrite decomposes into nitrogen and water even at room temperature, and may explode at 60 to 70°C. It is classified as explosive with low sensitivity to shock and friction, which is exactly why it is never stored or handled in pure, isolated form.

sodium_amide_reactivity.label: Sodium amide reacts violently with water
sodium_amide_reactivity.note: Sodium amide reacts violently with water, and in poorly sealed containers exposed to limited air and moisture it can form explosive peroxide mixtures. It is handled under inert gas, not open air.

ethylene_oxide_carcinogen.label: Ethylene oxide is flammable and carcinogenic
ethylene_oxide_carcinogen.note: Ethylene oxide is a very flammable, carcinogenic, mutagenic, irritating and anaesthetic gas, carrying GHS hazard codes for cancer risk (H350) and reproductive harm (H360FD). The same reactivity that makes it useful for sterilising hospital equipment is what makes it dangerous to handle directly.

bromate_carcinogen.label: Bromate is a suspected carcinogen
bromate_carcinogen.note: Bromate is a suspected human carcinogen; the US EPA caps it at 10 parts per billion in drinking water. Its presence in bottled water has forced product recalls.

chlorate_oxidizer.label: Potassium chlorate is a powerful oxidizer
chlorate_oxidizer.note: Potassium chlorate reacts vigorously, and in some cases spontaneously ignites or explodes, when mixed with combustible materials — sugar, sulfur and phosphorus among them. It is why safety matches keep the oxidizer in the striking strip and the fuel in the match head, never combined loose.

hydrazine_toxicity.label: Hydrazine is corrosive, toxic, and probably carcinogenic
hydrazine_toxicity.note: Hydrazine causes skin sensitization and respiratory irritation on contact, damages the liver and kidneys, and is rated by IARC as probably carcinogenic to humans, with occupational exposure linked to lung cancer. It also reacts with certain oxidizers on contact, no spark needed, which is exactly why it flies spacecraft.

violent_hydrolysis.label: These react violently with water
violent_hydrolysis.note: Phosphorus pentachloride and potassium oxide both tear themselves apart on contact with water — PCl5 back into phosphoric and hydrochloric acid, K2O into caustic potassium hydroxide — releasing heat fast enough to spatter and burn.

hexane_neurotoxicity.label: Chronic hexane exposure damages nerves
hexane_neurotoxicity.note: Chronic occupational exposure to n-hexane vapor is a documented cause of peripheral neuropathy — nerve damage recorded in auto mechanics, and in printing, shoe and furniture workers who use it as a solvent.

bleach_mixing_hazard.label: Never mix bleach with acid or ammonia
bleach_mixing_hazard.note: Sodium hypochlorite bleach releases toxic chlorine gas when mixed with an acid — vinegar included — and releases toxic chloramine gases when mixed with ammonia or urine. Both are real causes of acute lung injury from ordinary household cleaning.

dmso_skin_penetration.label: DMSO carries whatever is dissolved in it through skin
dmso_skin_penetration.note: DMSO increases how fast other compounds absorb through skin, so contaminants, toxins or medicines dissolved in it can be pulled into the body along with it — part of why handling it calls for butyl rubber or fluoroelastomer gloves rather than ordinary nitrile ones.

peanut_allergy.label: Peanut allergy can be fatal, and trace amounts are enough
peanut_allergy.note: Peanut allergy is a real IgE-mediated immune reaction, not a matter of taste — in a sensitised person even trace cross-contact from shared manufacturing equipment can trigger a reaction, and it's a leading cause of fatal and near-fatal food-allergy incidents. That's why processed foods carry 'may contain peanuts' warnings even when peanuts are never an ingredient.

isocyanate_sensitization.label: Isocyanates are a leading cause of occupational asthma
isocyanate_sensitization.note: Isocyanates present respiratory hazards as particulates, vapors or aerosols, and both the dose and duration of exposure can trigger respiratory sensitization — occupational asthma that, once it develops, can be acutely fatal on re-exposure. Skin contact alone is also enough to sensitize someone. This is industrial chemistry behind polyurethane, not something to spray without the ventilation and protective equipment autobody shops are built around.

crystalline_silica_dust.label: Fine silica dust causes silicosis
crystalline_silica_dust.note: Inhaling finely divided crystalline silica dust lodges in the lungs and continuously irritates the tissue, causing silicosis, bronchitis or lung cancer, and heavy occupational exposure is also linked to autoimmune diseases like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. The risk is in the fine dust from grinding, cutting or blasting — sandblasting, stone-countertop work and furnace operations among them — not the solid material sitting still.

capsaicin_irritant.label: Capsaicin burns skin and eyes on contact
capsaicin_irritant.note: Handling hot peppers bare-handed puts capsaicin on your skin, and it stays there until it's actively removed — plain water barely touches it, since capsaicin dissolves in oil and alcohol, not water. Touch an eye afterward and it causes intense tearing, pain and spasm of the eyelid. Gloves while cutting, and washing hands with soap before they go anywhere near your face, are what actually work.

ptfe_fume_fever.label: Overheated PTFE releases toxic fumes
ptfe_fume_fever.note: PTFE is stable at cookware temperatures, but above roughly 260 °C it starts to decompose, and the fumes cause polymer fume fever -- flu-like symptoms from a few hours' exposure. The classic case is a pet bird, whose respiratory system is far more sensitive, dying from a dry, overheated non-stick pan in another room.

vinyl_chloride_carcinogen.label: Vinyl chloride monomer is a known human carcinogen
vinyl_chloride_carcinogen.note: Long-term exposure to vinyl chloride gas causes a rare liver cancer, angiosarcoma, first identified in PVC-plant workers in the 1970s. The finished PVC plastic is chemically stable and not itself considered carcinogenic this way -- the hazard belongs to the monomer.

pvc_combustion.label: Burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride
pvc_combustion.note: PVC produces hydrogen chloride, water and carbon dioxide when it burns. HCl gas is corrosive to lungs and eyes even in small concentrations, which is why PVC smoke is far more dangerous to breathe than the smoke from most other plastics.

diazonium_salt_explosive.label: Dry diazonium salts are explosive
diazonium_salt_explosive.note: Benzenediazonium chloride is dangerously explosive as a dry solid -- it is made cold, kept in solution, and used within the hour, never isolated dry. Swapping the counterion for tetrafluoroborate gives a shock-insensitive salt instead, which is the whole reason that detour exists.

acetonitrile_cyanide.label: Acetonitrile is metabolised into cyanide
acetonitrile_cyanide.note: The body converts acetonitrile into hydrogen cyanide, which is the actual source of its toxic effects — and because that conversion takes hours, poisoning symptoms are delayed rather than immediate. Acetonitrile-based nail-polish remover has caused fatal child poisonings, which is why it has been banned from cosmetics in the European Economic Area since 2000.

nitrous_oxide_misuse.label: Nitrous oxide misuse causes real nerve damage
nitrous_oxide_misuse.note: Recreational inhaling — from whipped-cream chargers as much as anywhere else — inactivates vitamin B12 by oxidising it, and heavy repeated use is neurotoxic: documented cases show peripheral neuropathy, gait problems and numbness that can become permanent if it continues untreated.

phenolphthalein_carcinogen.label: Phenolphthalein was pulled from laxatives over cancer risk
phenolphthalein_carcinogen.note: It was used as a laxative for over a century before regulators phased it out of over-the-counter products; it sits on the IARC's 'possibly carcinogenic to humans' list, and US brands that once contained it were reformulated with other active ingredients entirely.

barium_peroxide_hazard.label: Barium peroxide is an oxidiser, and barium compounds are toxic
barium_peroxide_hazard.note: As an oxidiser it can intensify a fire it's anywhere near, and it's harmful if swallowed or inhaled in its own right — the same reactivity that gives fireworks their green colour makes it a substance to keep away from anything that burns.

trichloroacetic_acid_corrosive.label: Trichloroacetic acid burns skin the same way in a clinic or a spill
trichloroacetic_acid_corrosive.note: It causes severe skin burns and eye damage on contact — the identical mechanism a dermatologist uses on purpose in a controlled chemical peel destroys tissue indiscriminately outside that setting, and it's toxic to aquatic life besides.

sulfur_trioxide_corrosive.label: Sulfur trioxide turns to sulfuric acid the instant it meets water
sulfur_trioxide_corrosive.note: It reacts violently with water — including the moisture already in air — to produce corrosive sulfuric acid on the spot, and it's a strong enough dehydrating agent to ignite organic material through the heat of that reaction alone.

hydrogen_peroxide_concentration.label: Hydrogen peroxide's hazard is almost entirely about concentration
hydrogen_peroxide_concentration.note: The 3% bottle in a bathroom cabinet is mild enough that it mostly just stings; above roughly 40% it meets the formal definition of an oxidiser hazard, and concentrations near 98% dissolve paper on contact. It's the same molecule at every strength — only the number on the label changes what it can do.

benzene_carcinogen.label: Benzene is a known human carcinogen
benzene_carcinogen.note: Long-term benzene exposure is linked to leukaemia and other blood cancers, and it's classified as carcinogenic to humans. It also suppresses the bone marrow's ability to make new blood cells, which is why workplace exposure limits are strict.

copper_sulfate_toxicity.label: Copper sulfate is toxic well below fungicide doses
copper_sulfate_toxicity.note: Copper(II) salts have an LD50 around 100 mg/kg, and copper sulfate was once dosed deliberately as an emetic until it was recognised as too toxic for that use. It remains a WHO poison-control antidote entry, not a home remedy.

camphor_toxicity.label: Camphor is a real paediatric poisoning risk
camphor_toxicity.note: As little as 3 to 5 mL of 20% camphor oil, or roughly 30 mg/kg, can be lethal to a small child, and seizures have started within five minutes of ingestion. Camphor accounts for thousands of US poison-centre calls a year, most involving children under six.

silver_nitrate_caustic.label: Silver nitrate burns and stains on contact
silver_nitrate_caustic.note: Historically called 'lunar caustic,' silver nitrate is corrosive enough to cauterise tissue on purpose, and it stains skin permanently black wherever it touches by depositing metallic silver in the flesh. It also reacts explosively with ethanol.

lpg_flammability.label: Butane and propane are pressurised, flammable gases
lpg_flammability.note: Both are the fuel behind lighters, camp stoves and bottled LPG, and both form an explosive mix with air across a wide concentration range. Leaked gas pooling in an enclosed space, not the flame itself, is what turns a leak into an explosion.

elderberry_raw.label: Only the flower is eaten raw
elderberry_raw.note: Elderflower itself — what cordial and pressé are made from — needs no cooking. Every other part of the elder plant is different: the raw berries, leaves, bark and stems carry cyanogenic glycosides and cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea if eaten without cooking first.

theobromine_pet_toxicity.label: Chocolate is toxic to dogs and cats
theobromine_pet_toxicity.note: Theobromine is mild in humans but animals metabolize it far more slowly. A human LD50 near 800 mg/kg compares to roughly 300 mg/kg in dogs and 200 mg/kg in cats — dark and baking chocolate carry the highest doses.

glycyrrhizin_hypertension.label: Liquorice root can raise blood pressure
glycyrrhizin_hypertension.note: Glycyrrhizin blocks the enzyme that breaks down cortisol, and enough of it over enough time causes real sodium retention, potassium loss and high blood pressure — the FDA's own threshold sits around 0.2 mg per kilogram of body weight a day. Large amounts during pregnancy are linked to premature birth, so liquorice root is best avoided then.

fenugreek_pregnancy.label: Fenugreek seed and pregnancy don't mix
fenugreek_pregnancy.note: Fenugreek seed contains saponins that can act as a uterine stimulant, which is why it is considered unsafe in pregnancy. It can also lower blood sugar and interact with blood thinners — not as harmless as a kitchen spice sounds.

allyl_isothiocyanate_irritant.label: Allyl isothiocyanate is a lachrymatory irritant
allyl_isothiocyanate_irritant.note: The same compound that gives mustard, wasabi and horseradish their sting activates pain and irritant receptors directly — concentrated mustard oil is a genuine eye and skin irritant, not just a strong flavour.

safrole_carcinogen.label: Safrole was banned as a food additive in 1960
safrole_carcinogen.note: Ordinary cooking with nutmeg or mace is not the concern here. Safrole, a minor compound in both, proved to cause liver tumours in rats at high, sustained doses, and the US FDA banned it outright as a food additive in 1960 — long before sassafras root beer switched to a safrole-free extract.

glycyrrhizin_arrhythmia.label: Black liquorice and the FDA's 2 oz warning
glycyrrhizin_arrhythmia.note: Glycyrrhizin, liquorice's sweet compound, can drive down blood potassium. The FDA has warned that eating 2 oz of black liquorice a day for at least two weeks — if you're 40 or older — can bring on an irregular heartbeat; the effect is usually reversible once you stop.

poppy_seed_opiate_residue.label: Poppy seeds carry real trace opiates
poppy_seed_opiate_residue.note: Poppy seed hulls can be contaminated with trace morphine and codeine left over from harvest, enough that eating poppy seed foods can produce a positive result on an opiate drug test — refined tests can usually tell the difference. It takes a large quantity, roughly 300 to 400 grams, brewed as tea to reach a pharmacologically significant dose.

rabies_exposure.label: Rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms start
rabies_exposure.note: Rabies virus travels from a bite along nerves to the brain over days to months, and once neurological symptoms appear the disease is almost always fatal; the only real protection is prompt post-exposure vaccination before that happens. It still kills an estimated 55,000 people a year worldwide.

staphylococcus_illness.label: Staph food poisoning survives the cooking that kills the bacterium
staphylococcus_illness.note: Staphylococcus aureus itself is destroyed by ordinary cooking, but the enterotoxin it made while growing in food beforehand is heat-stable and survives. Symptoms — nausea, vomiting, cramping — typically start within 1 to 6 hours and clear within a day.

listeriosis_risk.label: Listeria keeps growing in the refrigerator
