listeriosis_risk.note: Listeria monocytogenes is one of the few foodborne pathogens that multiplies at refrigeration temperatures. Infection is usually mild in healthy adults but carries a 20-30% fatality rate in high-risk groups, and in pregnancy it can cause miscarriage or stillbirth.

campylobacteriosis_illness.label: Campylobacter is the most common bacterial foodborne illness in the US
campylobacteriosis_illness.note: Most Campylobacter infections resolve within about a week without treatment, but roughly 1 in 3,000 go on to trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome, an autoimmune nerve disorder, weeks after the diarrhea has cleared.

aflatoxin_carcinogen.label: Aflatoxin is one of the most potent liver carcinogens known
aflatoxin_carcinogen.note: Produced by Aspergillus flavus on stored peanuts and grain, aflatoxin B1 damages the p53 tumor-suppressor gene directly and is linked to liver cancer with chronic exposure, which is why the FDA caps it at 20 parts per billion in food.

clostridial_wound_risk.label: Deep wounds and soil are a real combination
clostridial_wound_risk.note: Clostridium tetani and Clostridium perfringens are both anaerobic soil bacteria that thrive specifically where a wound seals off oxygen. Tetanus causes spreading muscle rigidity that starts with lockjaw; gas gangrene causes outright muscle tissue death that can progress to shock within hours. Both are why puncture wounds and deep cuts get medical attention rather than just a bandage.

tick_borne_rickettsia.label: A tick bite can carry more than an itch
tick_borne_rickettsia.note: Rickettsia rickettsii is transmitted into the bloodstream by tick salivary secretions, and can start infecting a person in a feeding time as short as two hours. Before antibiotics were available, Rocky Mountain spotted fever killed more than 1 in 10 people it infected; with early treatment, mortality drops to about 1 in 200.

rubella_pregnancy_risk.label: Mild in most people, dangerous for a fetus
rubella_pregnancy_risk.note: Rubella is generally a mild disease with a light rash. The real danger is congenital: the virus can cross the placenta and interrupt fetal cell development, and infection early in pregnancy carries a high risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious birth defects.

gi_infection_risk.label: Fecal-oral pathogens are a real category
gi_infection_risk.note: Norovirus, hepatitis A, Cyclospora and Salmonella Typhi all spread the same basic way: something that touched contaminated feces reaches someone's mouth, often through food or water. Most cases resolve on their own, but typhoid fever and severe C. difficile colitis can turn genuinely serious.

bite_wound_zoonoses.label: An animal bite or scratch is a real inoculation
bite_wound_zoonoses.note: Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease) and Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever) both live in ordinary, often-healthy pets and rodents, and both cross into a person through a scratch or bite. Most cases are mild in a healthy adult, but rat-bite fever in particular can produce genuinely high, prostrating fevers.

gonorrhea_sti.label: A common bacterial STI, often silent
gonorrhea_sti.note: Neisseria gonorrhoeae infects an estimated 88 million people worldwide each year. About half of infected women and many infected men have no symptoms at all, yet untreated infection can still scar the fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease or infertility.

chlamydia_sti.label: The most-reported bacterial STI in the US
chlamydia_sti.note: Chlamydia trachomatis infected an estimated 61 million people worldwide in 2015. It's called the 'silent epidemic' because about 70% of infected women and half of infected men have no symptoms, which is why routine screening is recommended for sexually active people under 25.

syphilis_sti.label: Syphilis can imitate other diseases for years
syphilis_sti.note: Treponema pallidum caused an estimated 6 million new infections and about 107,000 deaths worldwide in 2015. Its early sores are often painless and easy to miss, and an untreated infection can resurface years later to damage the heart, brain, and blood vessels.

chancroid_sti.label: A painful genital ulcer disease, rare in wealthy countries
chancroid_sti.note: Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, common in some low-resource settings but only around one case per two million people a year in the US, UK, and similar countries. Its open sores substantially raise the risk of acquiring HIV during sex with an infected partner.

toxic_shock_risk.label: Toxic shock syndrome can turn fatal within hours
toxic_shock_risk.note: Certain Staphylococcus aureus strains release TSST-1, a superantigen that can trigger a cytokine storm, a sharp blood-pressure crash, and multi-organ failure. US incidence fell to roughly 0.3 to 0.5 cases per 100,000 people a year after high-absorbency tampons tied to the 1980 epidemic were pulled from the market, but the illness can still be fatal within hours if untreated.

leptospirosis_exposure.label: Leptospirosis spreads through water contaminated with animal urine
leptospirosis_exposure.note: Leptospira interrogans causes an estimated one million infections and about 58,900 deaths worldwide each year, mostly in the tropics. The bacteria enter through mucous membranes or breaks in the skin and can persist for weeks in warm, moist soil or fresh water fouled by the urine of infected rodents and livestock.

pyelonephritis_risk.label: Untreated bladder infections can spread to the kidneys
pyelonephritis_risk.note: Bacterial cystitis usually stays confined to the bladder, but if the causative bacteria ascend the ureters they can cause pyelonephritis, a kidney infection affecting an estimated 1 to 2 women per 1,000 each year. Among people over 65, the risk of death from untreated pyelonephritis is around 40%.

tetanus_illness.label: Tetanus is rare today because of vaccination, not luck
tetanus_illness.note: Clostridium tetani spores live in ordinary soil and dust and can enter through any deep or dirty wound. Tetanospasmin, the toxin it produces, kills roughly 1 in 10 who develop the disease. Routine childhood vaccination and decade boosters have cut US cases to under 40 a year, almost all in people who were never vaccinated.

botulism_illness.label: A different toxin, a different paralysis, from a namesake genus
botulism_illness.note: Clostridium botulinum causes true botulism, distinct from the food-preservation hazard of the same name — its toxin travels through the bloodstream to block nerve signals at the neuromuscular junction. Even treated it kills 5 to 10% of those affected; untreated, closer to half.

bacterial_meningitis.label: The bacterial form of a name that also covers a mild virus
bacterial_meningitis.note: Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae cause most bacterial meningitis, and even treated it kills roughly one in six patients. If the bacteria reach the bloodstream instead of, or alongside, the meninges, meningococcemia can follow — untreated, that form kills up to 80%. Conjugate vaccines exist against several of the major serotypes.

viral_encephalitis.label: Brain inflammation is a different order of danger than meningitis
viral_encephalitis.note: Untreated herpes simplex encephalitis kills about 70% of those it strikes, and even with antiviral treatment a third still die. Epidemic arboviral encephalitis varies enormously by virus, from under 1% case-fatality for La Crosse virus to 30–75% for eastern equine encephalitis.

sepsis_deaths.label: Sepsis is not rare, and it kills fast
sepsis_deaths.note: Sepsis affected an estimated 49 million people worldwide in 2017 and caused about 11 million deaths — one in five deaths worldwide that year. It is the body's own dysregulated inflammatory response to infection that does the damage, not the microbe directly, and if blood pressure will not recover with fluids alone it becomes septic shock, which carries a mortality rate near 40%.

plague_mortality.label: Plague still occurs, and pneumonic plague is nearly always fatal untreated
plague_mortality.note: The WHO still receives roughly 1,000 to 2,000 reported plague cases a year. Prompt antibiotics matter: untreated bubonic plague is usually fatal, and untreated pneumonic plague kills close to 100% of those infected, sometimes within days.

tularemia_infectivity.label: A handful of organisms is enough for some routes
tularemia_infectivity.note: Francisella tularensis is infectious enough that laboratory exposure alone has caused cases, part of why it is classified as a Tier 1 select agent. Before antibiotics, tularemia's severe forms killed up to 60% of untreated cases; treated today, mortality is under 4%.

aids_untreated_progression.label: Untreated HIV disease is fatal, though slowly
aids_untreated_progression.note: An estimated 40.9 million people were living with HIV worldwide in the most recent count, and AIDS-related illness still killed roughly 570,000 people that year — far below the epidemic's peak, thanks to antiretroviral therapy that suppresses but never eliminates the virus. Without treatment, HIV infection typically progresses to AIDS over three to twenty years.

hiv_opportunistic_infections.label: AIDS-defining infections turn dangerous only once CD4+ counts collapse
hiv_opportunistic_infections.note: Pneumocystis pneumonia, cytomegalovirus retinitis, toxoplasmic encephalitis, and Kaposi's sarcoma are all caused by organisms many people already carry harmlessly; they become life-threatening specifically once a person's CD4+ T cell count falls to roughly 200 cells per microliter or below. Before antiretroviral therapy, these opportunistic conditions were the leading causes of death in people with AIDS.

hiv_transmission_routes.label: HIV spreads through specific body-fluid routes, not casual contact
hiv_transmission_routes.note: HIV transmits via blood, semen, vaginal secretions, and breast milk — not through insect bites, saliva, or casual contact. A single needlestick from HIV-infected blood carries about a 0.3% infection risk, and untreated mother-to-child transmission occurs in roughly 20% to 35% of cases, falling below 5% with antiretroviral treatment.

abscess_severity_by_site.label: Where an abscess forms decides how dangerous it is
abscess_severity_by_site.note: Over 90% of documented and cultured skin abscesses grow Staphylococcus aureus, and a skin abscess rarely results in death because it eventually breaks through the skin on its own — which is why drainage, not antibiotics, is the standard treatment for an uncomplicated one. The same walled-off pocket of infection inside the skull is a different illness: brain abscess still ends in death in about 10% of cases even with treatment, with roughly 70% of people recovering well.

actinomycosis_invasion.label: Ordinary mouth bacteria in the wrong tissue plane
actinomycosis_invasion.note: Actinomyces species live harmlessly in the mouth and gut until dental work, periodontal disease, a broken jaw or surgery lets them into oxygen-free tissue, where they form slowly spreading abscesses that drain the yellow clumps called sulfur granules. Cervicofacial, thoracic and abdominal forms all occur. It is still called the great masquerader because the mass it makes can be mistaken for a tumour, and response to penicillin is slow enough to take months.

adenovirus_infection.label: Adenovirus survives on surfaces that would kill most viruses
adenovirus_infection.note: Adenoviruses cause about 10% of respiratory infections in children and spread by respiratory droplets, aerosols and the faecal route, with onset two to fourteen days after exposure. They are unusually stable against disinfectants, adverse pH and drying, which is why outbreaks move through hospitals, nurseries, barracks, boarding schools and swimming pools. Most infections resolve on their own and treatment is supportive, but in people with weakened immune systems adenovirus can become life-threatening multi-organ disease.

anthrax_spore_persistence.label: Anthrax spores wait decades in the ground, and the inhaled form kills about half
anthrax_spore_persistence.note: Bacillus anthracis survives as a spore that has caused infection after 70 years in soil, and an inhaled lethal dose is on the order of 10,000 to 20,000 spores. Untreated cutaneous anthrax kills roughly a quarter of cases; inhalation anthrax kills 50 to 80% untreated and still around 45% with modern treatment, rising to 97% once the fulminant phase begins. At least 2,000 cases a year are reported worldwide, most from contact with infected livestock, hides or wool.

arboviral_disease_burden.label: Viruses that arrive by bite, and mostly have no drug against them
arboviral_disease_burden.note: Arboviruses cycle between biting arthropods and vertebrate hosts, and the group includes dengue, yellow fever, Zika, chikungunya, West Nile and tick-borne encephalitis. Dengue alone causes at least 50 million infections a year and is the most clinically important of them. No effective antiviral drugs exist for this group and antibiotics do nothing; treatment is supportive, aimed at complications such as brain swelling.

bacterial_vaginosis_risks.label: Common, often symptomless, and it raises the risk of other infections
bacterial_vaginosis_risks.note: Bacterial vaginosis affects an estimated 23 to 29% of reproductive-age women worldwide, and about half have no symptoms at all. It roughly doubles the risk of acquiring several sexually transmitted infections including HIV, is associated with up to a six-fold increase in HIV shedding, and in pregnancy is linked to premature rupture of membranes and preterm birth. Recurrence after antibiotic treatment runs as high as 80%.

brucellosis_exposure.label: Raw milk and a slaughterhouse cut are the usual routes in
brucellosis_exposure.note: Brucella is contracted mainly by drinking unpasteurized milk from infected animals, by handling infected animals directly, or by breathing aerosolized bacteria. The organisms survive well in aerosols and resist drying, which makes brucellosis one of the classic laboratory-acquired infections from handling a culture plate. Even with optimal antibiotic therapy, 5 to 15% of patients relapse.

clostridium_toxins.label: One genus, and some of the most potent toxins in biology
clostridium_toxins.note: Clostridium species are obligate anaerobes that ride out oxygen as endospores and make toxin once they reach sealed tissue or sealed food: C. tetani causes tetanus, C. perfringens and C. septicum gas gangrene, C. botulinum botulism. Botulinum toxin's estimated human median lethal dose is 1.3 to 2.1 nanograms per kilogram injected, the deadliest natural substance recorded in the chemical literature. Their close relative Clostridioides difficile, which fills the gut space antibiotics empty, caused about 453,000 US cases and 29,000 deaths in 2011, and its spores are untouched by alcohol hand rub.

coccidiosis_human_species.label: Most coccidia stay inside one host species; a few of them reach people
coccidiosis_human_species.note: Coccidiosis is largely an animal disease — Eimeria species are locked to poultry, cattle and rabbits and are not contagious to humans. The coccidians that do infect people, chiefly Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora and Cystoisospora belli, spread by the same fecal-oral route and develop inside the epithelial cells lining the small intestine. In healthy adults that usually means about a week of diarrhea; in AIDS patients it can run for weeks or months with weight loss, and recurs after treatment.

cyanotoxin_bloom.label: Blue-green blooms make liver and nerve toxins that boiling does not remove
cyanotoxin_bloom.note: Cyanobacteria produce microcystins, which bond covalently to the protein phosphatases PP1 and PP2A in liver cells, alongside neurotoxins such as anatoxin-a and saxitoxin. The cyclic structure makes them stable across a wide range of temperature and pH, so boiling water does not clear them. At a dialysis clinic in Caruaru, Brazil in 1996, microcystin-contaminated supply water left 116 of 131 patients ill, 100 of them in acute liver failure, and at least 52 dead.

dermatophyte_transmission.label: Ringworm passes between people, animals and shared surfaces
dermatophyte_transmission.note: Dermatophytes may infect up to 20% of the world's population at any given time. They spread by direct contact with an infected person or animal and by contaminated objects — shared towels, clothing, footwear, hairbrushes, locker-room and pool floors, gym equipment left undisinfected. Topical antifungals usually clear an infection in one to two weeks, with treatment continued about a week past the last visible sign because the fungus outlasts the rash.

diphtheria_toxin_lethality.label: The membrane in the throat is not what kills
diphtheria_toxin_lethality.note: Corynebacterium diphtheriae spreads through the air from coughs and sneezes, and symptoms appear two to five days later. Its toxin travels in the blood to the heart and nerves, causing myocarditis and paralysis: about 5 to 10% of diagnosed cases die even with treatment, and 40 to 50% of untreated ones. In 2015 there were 4,500 reported cases and 2,100 deaths worldwide, in a disease the toxoid vaccine had largely removed from vaccinated populations.

ebv_lifelong_infection.label: Almost everyone carries it, and it never entirely leaves
ebv_lifelong_infection.note: About 95% of people have been infected with Epstein-Barr virus by age 40, usually via saliva, with symptoms appearing roughly 33 to 49 days later. Most recover from mononucleosis in two to four weeks, though fatigue lasts more than a month in an estimated 28% of cases and splenic rupture occurs in under 1%. The virus persists in B cells for life and is linked to Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinoma, and to multiple sclerosis.

endocarditis_mortality.label: An infection on a heart valve kills about one in four
endocarditis_mortality.note: Infective endocarditis occurs in roughly 3 to 9 people per 100,000 a year in developed countries; in-hospital mortality is about 18% and overall risk of death about 25%. Staphylococcus aureus causes around 31% of cases. As many as half of patients throw septic emboli, which is how a valve infection becomes a stroke, a kidney infarct or a mycotic aneurysm. Injection drug use, prosthetic valves and previously damaged valves are the main predisposing factors.

endotoxin_shock.label: Killing the bacterium does not remove the endotoxin
endotoxin_shock.note: Lipopolysaccharide binds the CD14/TLR4/MD2 receptor complex on monocytes and macrophages, which pour out inflammatory cytokines; a dose of 1 microgram per kilogram induces shock in a human, while a mouse tolerates a thousand times more. It is shed continuously in outer membrane vesicles as well as when cells lyse, and it is not destroyed by ordinary sterilization — full breakdown takes temperatures above 300°C, which is why pharmaceutical water is tested for it separately.

epidemic_typhus_lice.label: Rickettsia arrives on ticks, mites, fleas and lice, and typhus still follows war and famine
epidemic_typhus_lice.note: Rickettsia are obligate intracellular bacteria that cannot live outside a host cell, delivered by arthropods — ticks and mites for the spotted fever group, lice and fleas for the typhus group. Epidemic typhus, caused by R. prowazekii, is transmitted when louse faeces are scratched into the bite wound; untreated it kills about 40% of those infected, and close to none when antibiotics start within eight days. The louse-borne epidemic in Russia between 1918 and 1922 caused 2 to 3 million deaths among 20 to 30 million cases.

exotoxin_potency.label: Proteins potent enough that the disease is the toxin
exotoxin_potency.note: Exotoxins are secreted bacterial proteins, and the illness they cause is often entirely their doing: Clostridium botulinum, Clostridium tetani and Corynebacterium diphtheriae all work this way. AB toxins — cholera, pertussis, Shiga — use one subunit to bind the cell and another to act enzymatically inside it. Superantigens from Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes bridge MHC class II to the T-cell receptor and can activate up to 50% of a person's T cells at once, which is what toxic shock syndrome is. Heat or chemical treatment inactivates most of them into toxoids, the basis of the DPT vaccine.

group_a_strep_sequelae.label: Strep throat is minor; what group A strep does afterwards is not
group_a_strep_sequelae.note: Streptococcus pyogenes causes an estimated 700 million infections a year, and though overall mortality is under 0.1%, the 650,000-odd invasive cases — necrotizing fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock — kill about a quarter of the people they strike. Untreated throat infection carries a roughly 3% risk of acute rheumatic fever, which is why 33.4 million people now live with rheumatic heart disease. Antibiotics shorten the sore throat by only about 16 hours; what they change is the rheumatic fever risk.

healthcare_associated_infection.label: Care itself carries an infection rate
healthcare_associated_infection.note: WHO reports that out of every 100 patients in acute-care hospitals, seven in high-income countries and 15 in low- and middle-income countries acquire at least one health care-associated infection, and about one in ten of those patients dies of it. In the United States an estimated 687,000 such infections in 2015 contributed to 72,000 deaths. Catheter-associated urinary tract infection is the most common type at 32%, followed by surgical site infection at 22% and ventilator-associated pneumonia at 15%.

helicobacter_gastric_cancer.label: Most peptic ulcers are an infection, and a fraction of them end as cancer
helicobacter_gastric_cancer.note: Helicobacter pylori uses urease to split urea into ammonia and bicarbonate, neutralising the acid immediately around it, which lets it live in the stomach lining for decades and pass between people by saliva or the faecal-oral route. About two-thirds of the world's population carried it as of 2023; 10 to 20% of those infected develop peptic ulcers, and 1 to 3% develop gastric cancer over a lifetime against 0.13% in the never-infected. It is classed as a group 1 carcinogen and is behind roughly 89% of all gastric cancers.

herpes_simplex_persistence.label: Herpes simplex is lifelong, and it transmits with nothing visible to see
herpes_simplex_persistence.note: HSV settles into sensory nerve cells and reactivates for the rest of a person's life; WHO estimates 3.8 billion people under 50 carry HSV-1 and 520 million aged 15 to 49 carry HSV-2. It passes through oral, genital and skin contact, including when no sore is present. Most infections stay mild, but neonatal herpes occurs in about 10 of every 100,000 births and can cause neurological disability or death, and HSV-2 infection raises the risk of acquiring HIV roughly threefold.

hpv_cervical_cancer.label: Nearly every cervical cancer begins as an HPV infection
hpv_cervical_cancer.note: HPV is a sexually transmitted infection that almost everyone sexually active acquires at some point, usually without symptoms, and about 90% of infections clear within two years. The minority that persist can progress to cancer over a decade or more: nearly all cervical cancer is HPV-associated, and types 16 and 18 alone account for 70% of it. WHO counted roughly 660,000 new cervical cancer cases and 350,000 deaths worldwide in 2022.

impetigo_contagion.label: A skin infection that moves between children on contact
impetigo_contagion.note: Impetigo affected about 140 million people in 2010, most of them children aged two to five, and it spreads by direct contact with the lesions or with a nasal carrier of Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Untreated cases usually clear in about three weeks, but cellulitis and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, a kidney complication, can follow. Folliculitis and the boils that grow out of it trace to the same staphylococcus.

influenza_severity.label: Seasonal flu kills hundreds of thousands of people every year
influenza_severity.note: Influenza spreads in respiratory droplets and aerosols from breathing, talking, coughing and sneezing, with symptoms appearing one to four days after exposure. WHO puts the seasonal toll at around a billion infections a year, 3 to 5 million severe cases, and 290,000 to 650,000 deaths. Adults over 65 and infants under one carry most of that risk, and 30 to 40% of those hospitalised with influenza go on to develop pneumonia.

legionnaires_outbreak.label: Legionella arrives in aerosolized water, never from another person
legionnaires_outbreak.note: Legionella lives inside amoebae in warm plumbing, cooling towers and spa pools, and infects people who inhale contaminated mist two to ten days before symptoms start; it does not spread person to person. Legionnaires' disease kills around 10% of previously healthy people infected in the community and up to 25% of those with underlying conditions, with hospital-acquired cases near 28%. The 1976 Philadelphia convention outbreak that named it produced 182 reported cases and 29 deaths.

leishmaniasis_burden.label: Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is fatal in more than 95% of cases
leishmaniasis_burden.note: Leishmania parasites are transmitted by the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. The visceral form runs to 50,000 to 90,000 new cases a year worldwide and kills over 95% of those left untreated; the cutaneous form, at 600,000 to 1 million new cases a year, leaves ulcers and permanent scarring instead. WHO describes the disease as tracking malnutrition, displacement and poor housing rather than geography alone.

leprosy_nerve_damage.label: Leprosy is curable, but the nerve damage it does before treatment is permanent
leprosy_nerve_damage.note: Mycobacterium leprae passes only through prolonged close contact with an untreated case, in droplets from the nose and mouth; around 95% of people exposed never develop the disease, and the average incubation is about five years, occasionally as long as twenty. WHO recorded 182,815 new cases in 2023, of which 9,729 already had grade-2 visible disability by the time they were found. Multidrug therapy, supplied free by WHO, cures the infection in six months for paucibacillary and twelve for multibacillary disease, but loss of sensation and paralysis already caused do not reverse.

measles_severity.label: Measles killed an estimated 95,000 people in 2024, mostly children under five
measles_severity.note: One case can generate up to 18 secondary infections, and nine in ten non-immune people sharing a home with a case catch it. About 6% develop pneumonia; blindness, severe diarrhoea and brain inflammation also follow. Around 2 in 10,000 measles cases later develop subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a degenerative brain disease that appears on average ten years after the infection and is essentially always fatal.

mould_spore_exposure.label: Mould spores are harmless to most lungs and dangerous to a few
mould_spore_exposure.note: People inhale thousands of Aspergillus spores a day with no effect, because a working immune system clears them. Where it cannot — transplant recipients, people on steroids or other immunosuppressants — the same spores cause invasive aspergillosis, which affects around 300,000 people worldwide and carries 20% mortality at six months. Damp buildings also carry an allergic burden: as many as 21% of asthma cases have been attributed to mould exposure.

mrsa_resistance.label: MRSA is ordinary staph that the beta-lactam antibiotics no longer touch
mrsa_resistance.note: The mecA gene gives Staphylococcus aureus an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, that keeps cross-linking the cell wall while methicillin and its relatives sit bound to everything else. The US CDC estimates about 80,461 invasive MRSA infections and 11,285 deaths a year, and MRSA bloodstream infection carries close to twice the odds of death of the drug-susceptible form. It moves by skin contact, shared equipment and unwashed hands, and roughly 2% of people carry it in the nose without symptoms.

mucormycosis_risk.label: Bread mould, and in the wrong patient an infection that kills about half
mucormycosis_risk.note: The Mucorales — Rhizopus and Mucor, the moulds on spoiled bread and fruit — are inhaled harmlessly by almost everyone, but invade tissue and blood vessels in people with poorly controlled diabetes, particularly diabetic ketoacidosis, and in transplant recipients and those on long-term corticosteroids. Mucormycosis is fatal in about half of sinus cases, around two-thirds when it reaches the lungs, and nearly all disseminated cases. India confirmed over 40,845 cases and 3,129 deaths by 28 June 2021, 85.5% of them following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

mumps_complications.label: The swollen glands pass; some of the complications do not
mumps_complications.note: Mumps virus is shed in saliva from about a week before symptoms to eight days after, and incubates 16 to 18 days on average. Orchitis occurs in 10 to 40% of pubertal and post-pubertal males who catch it, aseptic meningitis in 5 to 10% of cases, and hearing loss in about 4% — permanent in roughly 1 infection in 20,000. The overall case-fatality rate is 1.6 to 3.8 per 10,000.

mycoplasma_pneumonia_illness.label: No cell wall means penicillin has nothing to attack
mycoplasma_pneumonia_illness.note: Mycoplasma pneumoniae spreads by respiratory droplets and aerosols and causes atypical pneumonia, the 'walking pneumonia' that reportedly accounts for 10 to 15% of community-acquired pneumonia overall and closer to 27% in children. Because the genus has no cell wall at all, beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin have no target and do nothing. Most infections stay mild, but the immune response can spill over into Guillain-Barré syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, haemolytic anaemia or encephalitis.

naegleria_infection.label: It enters through the nose, and almost no one survives it
naegleria_infection.note: Naegleria fowleri lives in warm fresh water and grows at temperatures up to 46°C. Infection happens only when water is forced up the nose — swallowing contaminated water does not cause it — after which the amoeba travels to the brain and causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. Symptoms appear one to twelve days after exposure, death usually follows within about two weeks, and the fatality rate is over 97% even with treatment; the US recorded 29 infections in the decade to 2022.

peptic_ulcer_complications.label: An ulcer that erodes into an artery is a surgical emergency
peptic_ulcer_complications.note: There were about 87.4 million new peptic ulcers and 267,500 deaths worldwide in 2015, and roughly 10% of people develop one at some point. Bleeding occurs in as many as 15% of cases and carries a 5 to 10% death rate; a posterior gastric ulcer perforating into the gastroduodenal artery kills about 20%. Eradicating Helicobacter pylori changed the disease from a chronic condition into a curable one — quadruple and bismuth-based regimens clear it in around 90% of cases.

pertussis_infant_risk.label: In infants the cough is the least of it
pertussis_infant_risk.note: About half of infected children under one year old are hospitalized, and roughly 1 in 200 of them dies. Pertussis caused an estimated 58,700 deaths worldwide in 2015, down from 138,000 in 1990. The paroxysms typically last one to six weeks and sometimes ten or more; the acellular vaccine is 71 to 85% effective, which is why adult and adolescent cases still circulate around infants too young to be fully immunized.

pneumococcal_disease.label: Carried harmlessly by millions, and still one of the great child killers
pneumococcal_disease.note: Streptococcus pneumoniae sits in the nose and throat of 5 to 10% of healthy adults and 20 to 40% of healthy children without causing anything. When it does invade it accounts for 15 to 50% of community-acquired pneumonia, and estimates of the child deaths it causes worldwide each year run from 700,000 to a million, most of them under five. Of about 30,000 US invasive cases in 2015, 30% were resistant to one or more antibiotics.

poliomyelitis_paralysis.label: Most polio infections show nothing at all; a small fraction paralyse permanently
poliomyelitis_paralysis.note: Poliovirus travels the faecal-oral route through water fouled by sewage, and about three quarters of infections produce no symptoms while the infected person stays contagious for up to six weeks. Between 0.1% and 0.5% of infections progress to paralytic polio, which kills 2 to 5% of children and 15 to 30% of adults, usually through paralysis of the respiratory muscles. Vaccination brought cases from an estimated 350,000 in 1988 down to 30 confirmed in 2022, but wild poliovirus still circulates in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

prion_disease.label: No genome, no treatment, and routine sterilization does not destroy it
prion_disease.note: A prion is a misfolded protein that converts normal copies of the same protein into its own shape, and every known prion disease is untreatable and fatal. Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease occurs at roughly 1 to 1.5 cases per million people a year, and about 70% of patients die within a year of diagnosis; variant CJD, from BSE-infected beef, has reached 178 UK cases as of 2024. Prions resist proteases, ionizing radiation and formaldehyde, surgical instruments have transmitted the disease through standard decontamination, and even 134°C for 18 minutes in a pressurized autoclave is only partly effective.

pseudomonas_hospital_infection.label: One in ten hospital-acquired infections, and hard to kill
pseudomonas_hospital_infection.note: Pseudomonas aeruginosa accounts for about one in ten hospital-acquired infections, striking burn patients, people with cystic fibrosis, ventilated patients, neutropenic cancer patients and premature infants. The WHO ranks it among the greatest antibiotic-resistance threats to humans: multidrug efflux pumps, beta-lactamases, a poorly permeable cell envelope and biofilm formation each blunt a different line of attack, and it thrives in the damp corners of human-made environments.

pseudomonas_resistance.label: The organism that infects the patients other bacteria cannot reach
pseudomonas_resistance.note: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunist armed with a low-permeability envelope, efflux pumps and its own AmpC beta-lactamase, which leaves it intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics. It is the most common cause of infection in burn injuries and forms chronic biofilms in cystic fibrosis lungs. The US CDC counted about 32,600 multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa infections among hospitalized patients in 2017 and 2,700 deaths, and WHO ranks it among the greatest antibiotic-resistance threats.

psilocybe_galerina_confusion.label: The deadliest little brown mushroom grows in the same habit as the ones foragers hunt for
psilocybe_galerina_confusion.note: Galerina marginata carries the same amatoxins as the death cap — one study measured 78 to 244 micrograms per gram fresh weight, in some specimens more than in Amanita phalloides itself, against an estimated lethal dose near 0.1 mg per kilogram of body weight. Poisonings have happened exactly this way, with collectors taking it for the hallucinogenic Psilocybe stuntzii. Amatoxin illness is deceptive: vomiting and diarrhoea some hours after the meal, then an apparent recovery, then liver failure.

rabies_encephalitis_fatality.label: Once the virus reaches the brain there is essentially no treatment
rabies_encephalitis_fatality.note: Rabies virus travels from the wound along nerve axons by retrograde transport, usually over one to three months but sometimes in under a week or after more than a year. Once encephalitis begins the disease is over 99% fatal; only about fourteen people were documented to have survived symptomatic rabies as of 2016. Vaccination given before symptoms appear prevents the disease, which is the whole reason post-exposure treatment is time-critical; some 59,000 people still die each year, more than 99% of them infected by dog bites.

sars_outbreak_mortality.label: SARS killed roughly one in ten of the people it infected
sars_outbreak_mortality.note: The 2002-2004 outbreak produced 8,096 confirmed cases and 783 known deaths, a case fatality rate near 11% that ranged from under 1% in people younger than 24 to over 50% in those aged 65 and older. It spread by respiratory droplets, aerosols and contaminated surfaces, with symptoms appearing four to six days after exposure. Human-to-human transmission was contained in 2003 and no case has been reported since 2004, though related coronaviruses persist in animal reservoirs.

scalded_skin_toxin.label: The bacterium stays put; the toxin that peels the skin travels
scalded_skin_toxin.note: Exfoliative toxins A and B from Staphylococcus aureus cleave desmoglein-1, the protein holding two epidermal layers together, so skin separates far from the site of infection itself. Most cases are in children under six, where mortality runs low — on the order of a few percent — but in adults, who develop it mainly alongside immunosuppression or kidney failure, reported mortality reaches 50 to 60%.

trachoma_blindness.label: Repeated infection scars the eyelid until the lashes turn inward
trachoma_blindness.note: Chlamydia are obligate intracellular bacteria that alternate an infectious form with a replicating one inside the host cell. In the eye, Chlamydia trachomatis causes trachoma, spread by hands, shared cloth and flies carrying discharge from an infected person's eyes or nose; repeated infection over years scars the inner eyelid until the lashes scrape the cornea. It is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, with about 1.9 million people blind or visually impaired by it and 92 million living where it is endemic.

trypanosomiasis_burden.label: Two parasites on two continents, both fatal if nothing is done
trypanosomiasis_burden.note: Trypanosoma brucei is injected by tsetse flies and causes human African trypanosomiasis, generally fatal untreated; sustained control has held reported cases under 1,000 a year since 2018, though about 55 million people still live where transmission is possible. Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by triatomine bugs and also passed in pregnancy, transfusion and contaminated food, infects an estimated 8 million people and causes more than 10,000 deaths a year. Up to a third of chronic Chagas infections eventually damage the heart.

tuberculosis_burden.label: Latent in a quarter of humanity, and still killing over a million people a year
tuberculosis_burden.note: Mycobacterium tuberculosis travels through the air from someone with active lung disease, and about a quarter of the world's population carries a latent infection that causes no symptoms and cannot be passed on. Between 5 and 10% of those infected go on to active disease. WHO counted an estimated 10.7 million new cases and 1.23 million deaths in 2024, and only about two in five people with multidrug-resistant TB reached treatment that year.

wart_transmission.label: A wart is a live viral infection, not a lump of dead skin
wart_transmission.note: Common warts are caused by human papillomavirus types 2 and 4 most often, with types 1, 3, 26, 29 and 57 also implicated, and the virus enters through a break in the skin. Non-genital warts are present in an estimated 1 to 13% of the general population, and public showers and pools are recognized risk settings. Most resolve on their own over months to years; a weakened immune system makes them more numerous and more persistent.

west_nile_neuroinvasive.label: Silent in most people, neuroinvasive in a few
west_nile_neuroinvasive.note: About 80% of West Nile infections produce no symptoms at all, and fewer than 1% reach the nervous system as meningitis or encephalitis — but among those, roughly 10% die, and survivors can spend 60 to 90 days recovering with motor deficits and fatigue lasting more than a year. Mosquitoes carry it; blood transfusion, organ transplant and mother-to-child transmission are documented but uncommon. There is no human vaccine.

yellow_fever_toxic_phase.label: The fever that comes back is the dangerous one
yellow_fever_toxic_phase.note: Yellow fever begins three to six days after the mosquito bite, and in about 15% of people the fever returns within a day of apparent recovery — the toxic phase, with jaundice, bleeding and organ failure. Among those who become jaundiced, 20 to 50% die. The WHO estimates 200,000 cases a year, about 90% of them in Africa. A single dose of vaccine protects 95% of recipients from day 10 onward and is now considered to confer lifelong immunity.

aflatoxin_in_storage.label: Groundnuts and maize grow the most potent liver carcinogen known if they are stored warm and damp
aflatoxin_in_storage.note: Aspergillus flavus grows on stored groundnuts, maize, tree nuts and spices wherever moisture reaches about 7% and the temperature sits between 13 and 40°C, and it produces aflatoxin. Naturally occurring aflatoxins are an IARC Group 1 carcinogen, and somewhere between 5 and 28% of the world's liver cancer is attributed to them. The risk multiplies with hepatitis B: infected and exposed together carries up to thirty times the risk of exposure alone, which is why the burden falls on sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia and China. Regulated markets test for it and cap it — the FDA limit is 20 parts per billion.

alcohol_carcinogen.label: Alcohol has been a Group 1 carcinogen since 1988
alcohol_carcinogen.note: IARC classified alcoholic beverages as carcinogenic to humans in 1988, and acetaldehyde — what the liver turns ethanol into — in 2009. It causes cancer of the mouth, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver, colon, rectum and breast. About 740,000 cancer cases in 2020, 4.1% of all new cases, were attributed to alcohol, more than three-quarters of them in men. There is no drink that is exempt: the risk follows the ethanol, not the kind of drink it arrives in.

processed_meat_carcinogen.label: Processed meat is a Group 1 carcinogen, in the same confidence class as tobacco
processed_meat_carcinogen.note: IARC classified processed meat — meat salted, cured, fermented or smoked to preserve it or change its flavour — as carcinogenic to humans in 2015. Every 50 grams eaten daily raises the risk of bowel cancer by about 18%, and roughly 34,000 cancer deaths a year worldwide are attributed to diets high in it. Group 1 describes how certain the evidence is, not how dangerous the thing is: tobacco sits in the same group and is estimated to kill about a million people a year.

red_meat_probable_carcinogen.label: Red meat is probably carcinogenic, on weaker evidence than processed meat
red_meat_probable_carcinogen.note: IARC places red meat — all mammalian muscle meat, so beef, veal, pork, lamb, mutton, horse and goat — in Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans. The association with bowel cancer is consistent but the evidence is not strong enough to call it causal: if it is, every 100 grams a day would raise the risk by about 17%, and some 50,000 cancer deaths a year would be attributable to it.

salted_fish_carcinogen.label: Chinese-style salted fish is a Group 1 carcinogen
salted_fish_carcinogen.note: IARC classifies Chinese-style salted fish as carcinogenic to humans, linked to nasopharyngeal cancer and to stomach cancer. The salting is what does it: the fish partially ferments before it dries, and the nitrites it carries can go on to form nitrosamines. Salting as a preservation method is not the same thing as this particular preparation.

carbon_monoxide_poisoning.label: Carbon monoxide gives no warning at all, and binds 240 times harder than oxygen
carbon_monoxide_poisoning.note: It is colourless, odourless and tasteless, so nothing about a room tells you it is filling with it. Haemoglobin holds carbon monoxide about 240 times more tightly than oxygen, so blood keeps circulating while carrying less and less of what it is for. 35 parts per million brings on headache and dizziness after six to eight hours; 1,600 ppm can kill in under two. It causes more than 400 non-fire deaths and 20,000 emergency visits a year in the United States alone. Burning charcoal indoors or in a tent is a common way people are poisoned, because a fire that looks small still produces it.

corium_lethality.label: Chernobyl's Elephant's Foot delivered a coin-flip lethal dose in about three minutes
corium_lethality.note: Corium is what a reactor core becomes after it melts and takes the concrete, sand, steel and zirconium around it with it. The mass under Reactor 4 was measured at 8,000 to 10,000 roentgens an hour when it was found in December 1986 — enough to deliver 4.5 grays, the dose that kills about half the people who receive it, in roughly three minutes of standing near it. It was too dense to drill, so the sample taken from it was cut out with armour-piercing rounds.

ethylene_glycol_poisoning.label: Antifreeze tastes sweet, which is most of the problem
ethylene_glycol_poisoning.note: Ethylene glycol is not very toxic in itself; alcohol dehydrogenase turns it into glycolic and then oxalic acid, and the oxalate binds calcium into crystals that lodge in the kidneys. About 1.4 mL per kilogram is a lethal dose, and deaths have followed as little as 30 mL of concentrate. The sweetness is why children and animals drink it in quantity, and why more than 5,000 poisonings a year are reported in the United States. Fomepizole works by blocking the enzyme before the conversion happens.

foxglove_cardiac_glycoside.label: Every part of a foxglove is poisonous, and drying does not change that
foxglove_cardiac_glycoside.note: Foxglove carries cardiac glycosides — digoxin and digitoxin — which inhibit the sodium-potassium pump in heart muscle and force it to contract harder. That is exactly why it became a heart drug and exactly why the plant is dangerous: the gap between a dose that helps and one that harms is very narrow. Poisoning brings vomiting, a heart that runs too fast or too slow, delirium, and the yellow-tinged vision with halos that is characteristic of it. Roots, leaves, flowers and seeds are all toxic, dried as well as fresh.

urushiol_contact.label: The oil in poison ivy is also in mango skin and cashew shell
urushiol_contact.note: Urushiol is a hapten: it soaks into skin within minutes and chemically alters the proteins it meets, so the immune system stops recognising them as yours. The rash is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to that alteration, not a burn or a poison. It runs through the whole cashew family — poison ivy, oak and sumac, the lacquer tree, mango leaves, skin and sap, and the shell around a raw cashew, which is why cashews are never sold in their shells. Over 90% of people react to the unsaturated form.

$severity: How loudly to say it. acute: can kill or permanently injure. contact: burns, corrodes or envenomates on contact. cumulative: harms with exposure over time. conditional: harms only some people, or only in some circumstances. The tier decides the signal on the card; it is never a ranking of how bad a thing is, and it is never advice.
